lessons.title: V3·DA1 — Minimal APIs, route groups and endpoint filters
lessons.summary: Minimal APIs are not a lightweight toy version of controllers; they are a different composition model. This sector takes the endpoint apart: how a delegate becomes a route, how MapGroup shares configuration without inheritance, and how endpoint filters wrap a single handler instead of the whole pipeline.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·DA1 — Minimal APIs, route groups and endpoint filters

You have mapped endpoints before. `app.MapGet("/things", Handler)` is muscle
memory by now, and sector 03 taught you the middleware pipeline that every one
of those requests passes through on its way in. This sector is about the part
between the two: the machinery that turns a C# delegate into an endpoint, the
object that lets fifty endpoints share one decision, and the filter that wraps
exactly one handler rather than the whole application.

The reason to care is that most real APIs go wrong in the same place. You start
with six endpoints and a clean `Program.cs`. Six months later there are ninety,
and every one of them repeats the same four lines: check the tenant header, look
up the caller's depot, stamp a correlation id, translate a domain exception into
a status code. Somebody notices, and reaches for the tool they know — middleware
— and now that logic runs for the health check, for the static files, and for
the OpenAPI document, and it cannot see which endpoint it is running in front of
because middleware runs before routing has finished making that decision.

Route groups and endpoint filters are the answer, and they are the answer
because of *where* they sit.

## Concept — the endpoint is a data structure

`MapGet` does not register a callback. It builds an `Endpoint`: a request
delegate, a display name, and a **metadata collection** — a bag of arbitrary
objects attached to the route. `RequireAuthorization` puts an
`AuthorizeAttribute` in that bag. `WithName` puts an `EndpointNameMetadata` in
it. `Produces<Dock>(200)` puts a `ProducesResponseTypeMetadata` in it. Nothing
reads the bag at map time; the routing middleware selects an endpoint, sets it
on `HttpContext`, and later components — the authorization middleware, the
OpenAPI generator, your own middleware calling `context.GetEndpoint()` — read the
metadata they care about and ignore the rest.

Two consequences follow, and both are load-bearing for this sector. First, order
of registration does not decide which route wins: **route matching is by
specificity**, not by declaration order. A literal segment beats a parameter
segment beats a catch-all, and a constrained parameter beats an unconstrained
one. `/v3da01/bikes/available` and `/v3da01/bikes/{id:int}` can be declared in
either order and `available` still wins, because `available` is more specific.
When two routes are *equally* specific, you do not get the first one — you get an
`AmbiguousMatchException` at request time, which is the router refusing to guess.

Second, because the endpoint is data, something can decorate it after the fact.
That is what a group is.

## Concept — MapGroup is a builder, not a namespace

```csharp
var docks = app.MapGroup("/v3da01/docks")
    .WithTags("depot")
    .AddEndpointFilter<AuditFilter>();

docks.MapGet("/", ListDocks);
docks.MapGet("/{id}", GetDock);
```

`MapGroup` returns a `RouteGroupBuilder`, which is itself an
`IEndpointRouteBuilder`. Endpoints mapped into it inherit the prefix and every
*convention* added to the group. A convention is a delegate that runs over each
endpoint's builder when the endpoint is finally built — which is at application
startup, not at map time. This is why you can add a convention to a group
**after** mapping endpoints into it and it still applies: nothing has been built
yet.

Groups nest, and the prefixes concatenate. A nested group inherits the parent's
conventions and can add its own. What it cannot do is *remove* one, which is the
first real design constraint: a group is an "everything in here also gets X"
statement, so if one endpoint in twenty needs to opt out, either it does not
belong in the group or the exception has to be expressible as metadata the
convention checks — the way `AllowAnonymous` works, as a piece of metadata that
authorization deliberately looks for and honours.

## Concept — the filter wraps the handler

An endpoint filter is the middleware idea applied one level down:

```csharp
app.MapPost("/v3da01/rides", StartRide)
   .AddEndpointFilter(async (context, next) =>
   {
       var started = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();
       var result = await next(context);
       context.HttpContext.Response.Headers["X-Elapsed-Ms"] =
           Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(started).TotalMilliseconds.ToString("F1");
       return result;
   });
```

Same shape as middleware — do work, `await next`, do work — and three
differences that matter:

- It runs **after** routing, model binding and argument construction. By the time
  your filter executes, the handler's parameters have been bound, and
  `context.GetArgument<T>(index)` hands you the typed object. Middleware cannot
  do that; middleware sees a stream.
- It returns an **object**, not `void`. Whatever `next` gives back is the
  handler's return value on its way to being serialised, and your filter can
  inspect it, replace it, or refuse to call `next` at all and return its own
  `IResult`. Short-circuiting is one `return TypedResults.Problem(...)`.
- It is attached to **one endpoint** (or one group), so it never runs for a
  request that was never going to reach that handler.

Ordering is where people get burned. Filters run in the order they are added,
and group filters are added before endpoint filters, so a group filter is
*outermost*: group filter start → endpoint filter start → handler → endpoint
filter end → group filter end. Nested groups extend the same nesting outward.
Say it as "outside in on the way down, inside out on the way back" and you will
predict it correctly every time.

## What this sector drills

You will build a bike-share depot API under `/v3da01/...` — docks, bikes, rides
— and take it from a flat pile of `MapGet` calls to a grouped, filtered,
strongly-typed surface. Exercise 1 and 2 are the routing layer: grouping, and the
precedence rules that decide which route wins. Exercises 3 to 5 are filters:
writing one, short-circuiting from one, and proving to yourself which order they
run in. Exercise 6 moves to a filter class with constructor injection that reads
a bound argument. Exercise 7 replaces `IResult` with a `Results<...>` union so
the compiler and the OpenAPI document both know what an endpoint can return.
Exercise 8 is `AddEndpointFilterFactory`, the escape hatch that inspects the
handler's `MethodInfo` at build time and decides whether to wrap it at all.

The challenge composes nested groups, a factory-built filter and a union return
type into one idempotent write endpoint. The review comes back later and asks
for the same ideas from the exception-translation angle.

One habit to carry in: whenever you are about to write a piece of cross-cutting
logic, ask *how much of the request does this need to see?* If the answer is "the
raw path", it is middleware. If the answer is "the bound arguments and the
result", it is an endpoint filter. Choosing the wrong one is not a style
mistake — it is the difference between code that can do its job and code that has
to re-parse the request to find out where it is.

# Reading - dotnet/v3da01_minimal_api_groups

Minimal APIs shipped in .NET 6 as a smaller way to write an endpoint. Route
groups and endpoint filters arrived in .NET 7 and turned them into a composition
model. These are the mechanisms behind that, and the places they bite.

## Notes

**`Map*` builds metadata; nothing executes at map time.** `MapGet` returns a
`RouteHandlerBuilder`, which accumulates *conventions* — delegates of the form
`Action<EndpointBuilder>`. `WithTags`, `RequireAuthorization`, `Produces` and
`AddEndpointFilter` all just append to that list. The conventions run once, when
`app.Build()` materialises the `EndpointDataSource`. This is why a convention
added after the `MapGet` line still applies, and why an exception thrown from a
convention surfaces at startup rather than on a request.

**Route matching is specificity-ordered, not declaration-ordered.** Each segment
gets a precedence: literal, then constrained parameter, then unconstrained
parameter, then catch-all. Segments are compared left to right. So
`/bikes/available` beats `/bikes/{id:int}` beats `/bikes/{id}` beats
`/bikes/{*rest}`, whatever order you wrote them in. Two routes with identical
precedence and no tiebreaker throw `AmbiguousMatchException` — at request time,
for that path only, which is why it is so often found in production rather than
in a build.

**Constraints filter candidates; they do not validate input.** `{id:int}` means
"this route only matches when the segment parses as an int". A request to
`/bikes/abc` with only that route registered is a **404**, not a 400, because no
endpoint matched. That is usually what you want for identifiers and almost never
what you want for a business rule — `{age:min(18)}` gives a confusing 404 to an
under-18, where a bound parameter and an explicit check gives a 400 that explains
itself. Use constraints for disambiguation, not for policy.

**`MapGroup` inherits forward, never backward.** A `RouteGroupBuilder` is an
`IEndpointRouteBuilder` *and* an `IEndpointConventionBuilder`. Conventions added
to the group apply to every endpoint mapped into it, including into nested
groups; conventions added to a single endpoint apply only there. Group prefixes
concatenate, and a group prefix may itself contain route parameters —
`MapGroup("/depots/{depotId}")` — which every handler inside can then bind.

**Filters run inside routing, outside the handler.** The filter pipeline is built
once per endpoint at startup by folding the registered factories into a chain
ending at the handler. Each link is
`EndpointFilterDelegate: (EndpointFilterInvocationContext) => ValueTask<object?>`.
Group filters wrap endpoint filters wrap the handler. Returning without calling
`next` short-circuits, and the object you return is the response.

**`context.GetArgument<T>(index)` is positional and unchecked.** The context
carries `IList<object?> Arguments` in the handler's parameter order.
`GetArgument<T>(0)` casts; get the index or the type wrong and you get an
`InvalidCastException` at request time. A filter that hard-codes index 0 is
coupled to a signature nobody will remember to keep in sync, which is exactly the
problem `AddEndpointFilterFactory` exists to solve.

**`Results<T1, T2>` is a compile-time union.** `TypedResults.Ok(dock)` has type
`Ok<Dock>`; `Results<Ok<Dock>, NotFound>` implicitly converts from either and
implements `IEndpointMetadataProvider`, so the OpenAPI document learns both
status codes without a single `Produces` call. Return plain `IResult` and the
document knows nothing.

## ex1 - the group is the unit of shared configuration

Everything the group carries — the prefix, the tag, the filter — is declared once
and applies to endpoints declared later. Note what you did *not* have to do:
there is no base class, no attribute, no `[Route]` on a type. The grouping is an
expression, so it can be built conditionally, passed to a method, or produced by
a loop over configuration.

The trap is thinking the prefix is cosmetic. `MapGroup("/v3da01/docks")` followed
by `MapGet("/")` produces `/v3da01/docks` (the trailing empty segment is elided),
while `MapGet("")` produces the same thing and `MapGet("/{id}")` produces
`/v3da01/docks/{id}`. Getting a stray slash into a group prefix gives you a route
that looks right in source and 404s in a browser.

## ex2 - precedence, and the 404 that should have been a 400

You registered `/bikes/{id:int}` and `/bikes/available` and proved the literal
wins regardless of order. The second half is more interesting: `/bikes/abc`
returns 404 because the constraint removed the only candidate. If a client is
sending you a malformed identifier, 404 is a defensible answer — the resource
genuinely is not there — but the moment the segment carries meaning beyond
identity, the constraint is hiding a validation error behind a "no such page".

## ex3 - your first filter, and why it is not middleware

Stamping a response header is deliberately trivial so that the wiring is the
lesson. The filter sees `context.HttpContext`, so anything middleware can do it
can also do; what it additionally sees is the bound arguments and the returned
result. It also *only runs for this endpoint*, which is the part that middleware
cannot express without a `context.GetEndpoint()` check and a metadata lookup you
would have to invent yourself.

## ex4 - short-circuiting is just an early return

`return TypedResults.Problem(...)` without calling `next` means the handler never
runs. Two details are worth internalising: the return type is `object?`, so
anything the result-writing machinery understands is legal; and the filters
*outside* you still get to run their tail code, because you returned to them
normally. A short circuit is not an exception — the outer filters see a result,
not a failure.

## ex5 - order, proved rather than remembered

Building the trace header from the group filter and the endpoint filter turns a
rule into an observation. Group first, endpoint second, handler, then unwinding
in reverse. Once you have seen the string `g1>e1>handler>e1<g1<`, the rule stops
being something you look up.

## ex6 - a filter class, DI, and reading the bound argument

`IEndpointFilter` as a class buys you constructor injection and a name in the
stack trace. Reading `GetArgument<RideRequest>(0)` is where a filter earns its
keep: the payload is already deserialised, so a validation filter costs nothing
extra and returns a properly-shaped 400 before the handler is entered.

## ex7 - the union type, and honest metadata

`Results<Ok<BikeDto>, NotFound, ValidationProblem>` makes the compiler enforce
that every path returns one of the declared shapes, and makes the OpenAPI
document say so without duplication. The cost is that adding a fourth outcome is
a signature change — which is the point. Silent additions to the set of things an
endpoint can return are how clients get surprised.

## ex8 - the factory, and build-time decisions

`AddEndpointFilterFactory` runs **once per endpoint at startup** and returns
either a filter delegate or `next` unchanged. Because it receives
`EndpointFilterFactoryContext.MethodInfo`, it can look at the handler's
parameters and decide. That gives you two wins at once: no per-request
reflection, and no filter at all on endpoints that do not need one.

## challenge - composition

Nested group, factory-built idempotency filter, union return type. The ordering
question — whether the idempotency check runs before or after validation — is the
design decision, and there is a defensible answer in the prompt.

## review1 - the same tools, aimed at exceptions

Translating a domain exception into a 409 inside a filter, rather than in global
exception handling, keeps the translation next to the endpoints that can raise
it. It also shows the last property of the filter chain: an exception thrown by
the handler propagates *outward* through the filters, so a `try`/`catch` around
`await next(context)` is a working, scoped exception handler.

## Further reading

- [Minimal APIs overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/overview)
- [Route groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/route-handlers#route-groups)
- [Filters in minimal API apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/min-api-filters)
- [Routing in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/routing)
- [Create responses in minimal API apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/responses)

# V3·DA1 — Minimal APIs, route groups and endpoint filters

The deep version. Read this once before the exercises and again after ex8, when
the parts have names you have actually used.

## 1. What `MapGet` really produces

An ASP.NET Core application is, at the routing layer, a list of `Endpoint`
objects. Each one carries:

- a `RequestDelegate` — the thing that finally runs,
- a `RoutePattern` — the template plus its constraints,
- an `EndpointMetadataCollection` — an untyped bag of objects,
- a display name, used in logs and diagnostics.

`MapGet("/docks/{id}", GetDock)` builds one of these, but not immediately. It
returns a `RouteHandlerBuilder` that accumulates **conventions**:

```csharp
var builder = app.MapGet("/v3da01/docks/{id}", GetDock);
builder.WithName("GetDock");                 // convention appended
builder.Produces<DockDto>(StatusCodes.Status200OK);   // convention appended
builder.AddEndpointFilter<AuditFilter>();    // convention appended
```

At `app.Build()`, every convention runs against an `EndpointBuilder`, the
metadata bag is filled, the filter pipeline is folded, and the `Endpoint` is
frozen. Two practical consequences:

```csharp
var group = app.MapGroup("/v3da01/docks");
group.MapGet("/", ListDocks);       // mapped first
group.WithTags("depot");            // added second - still applies
```

and, less happily, a convention that throws does so during startup, with a stack
trace that names the convention rather than your handler.

## 2. Route precedence, in the order the router applies it

Segment-by-segment, left to right, lower number wins:

| segment | example | precedence |
|---|---|---|
| literal | `available` | 1 |
| constrained parameter | `{id:int}` | 2 |
| unconstrained parameter | `{id}` | 3 |
| constrained catch-all | `{*rest:alpha}` | 4 |
| catch-all | `{*rest}` | 5 |

```csharp
app.MapGet("/v3da01/bikes/{id:int}", GetBike);
app.MapGet("/v3da01/bikes/available", ListAvailable);   // declared second, wins
```

`GET /v3da01/bikes/available` reaches `ListAvailable`. `GET /v3da01/bikes/7`
reaches `GetBike`. `GET /v3da01/bikes/abc` is a **404**: the `int` constraint
eliminated the only candidate and the literal did not match.

If you truly need to override precedence, `WithOrder(int)` exists. Reaching for
it is usually a sign that two routes are fighting over the same shape and one of
them should be a query parameter.

## 3. Groups

```csharp
var depot = app.MapGroup("/v3da01")
    .WithTags("depot");

var docks = depot.MapGroup("/docks")
    .AddEndpointFilter<AuditFilter>();

docks.MapGet("/", ListDocks);              // /v3da01/docks
docks.MapGet("/{id}", GetDock);            // /v3da01/docks/{id}
```

Rules worth memorising:

- Prefixes concatenate; conventions accumulate outward-in.
- A group prefix may contain parameters, and handlers inside bind them normally.
- There is no "remove convention" operation. Opting out has to be expressed as
  metadata the convention itself honours.
- `MapGroup("")` is legal and useful when you want shared conventions without a
  shared prefix.

## 4. Filters

```csharp
public class RideAuditFilter(ILogger<RideAuditFilter> logger) : IEndpointFilter
{
    public async ValueTask<object?> InvokeAsync(
        EndpointFilterInvocationContext context, EndpointFilterDelegate next)
    {
        var request = context.GetArgument<RideRequest>(0);
        if (request.Minutes <= 0)
        {
            return TypedResults.ValidationProblem(new Dictionary<string, string[]>
            {
                ["minutes"] = ["Must be positive."],
            });
        }

        var result = await next(context);
        logger.LogInformation("ride for {Bike} returned {Result}",
            request.BikeId, result?.GetType().Name);
        return result;
    }
}
```

The chain for an endpoint in a group with one group filter and one endpoint
filter:

```
group filter  ->  endpoint filter  ->  handler
              <-                   <-
```

Add a second endpoint filter and it goes *inside* the first. Add a nested group
and its filter goes between the outer group's and the endpoint's.

### The factory

```csharp
docks.AddEndpointFilterFactory((context, next) =>
{
    var takesRide = context.MethodInfo.GetParameters()
        .Any(p => p.ParameterType == typeof(RideRequest));

    if (!takesRide) return next;          // no filter at all for this endpoint

    return async invocation =>
    {
        var ride = invocation.Arguments.OfType<RideRequest>().Single();
        if (ride.Minutes <= 0) return TypedResults.BadRequest("minutes");
        return await next(invocation);
    };
});
```

The outer lambda runs once per endpoint at startup. The inner lambda is the
per-request filter. Returning `next` unchanged means "do not wrap this one",
which costs nothing at runtime.

## 5. Results and unions

`Results.Ok(x)` returns `IResult`. `TypedResults.Ok(x)` returns `Ok<T>` — a
concrete type. That difference is what makes unions possible:

```csharp
private static Results<Ok<BikeDto>, NotFound, ValidationProblem> GetBike(int id)
{
    if (id <= 0)
        return TypedResults.ValidationProblem(new Dictionary<string, string[]>
        {
            ["id"] = ["Must be positive."],
        });

    var bike = V3DA01Depot.Bikes.FirstOrDefault(b => b.Id == id);
    return bike is null
        ? TypedResults.NotFound()
        : TypedResults.Ok(BikeDto.From(bike));
}
```

The union implements `IEndpointMetadataProvider`, so 200, 404 and 400 all land in
the OpenAPI document with no `Produces` calls. Returning a shape not in the union
is a compile error.

## 6. Opting one endpoint out of a group convention

There is no `RemoveEndpointFilter`. The idiomatic escape is the pattern the
framework itself uses for `AllowAnonymous`: publish a marker as metadata, and
have the convention honour it.

```csharp
public sealed class SkipAudit;

var docks = app.MapGroup("/v3da01/docks")
    .AddEndpointFilter(async (context, next) =>
    {
        var endpoint = context.HttpContext.GetEndpoint();
        if (endpoint?.Metadata.GetMetadata<SkipAudit>() is not null)
        {
            return await next(context);      // opted out, do nothing extra
        }

        // ... audit ...
        return await next(context);
    });

docks.MapGet("/health", () => TypedResults.Ok()).WithMetadata(new SkipAudit());
```

The filter still runs — it is in the chain — but it declines to act. That is a
different thing from not being there, and on a hot path the difference is
measurable, so if the exemption is permanent, moving the endpoint out of the
group remains the better answer.

## 7. Common mistakes

1. **Using middleware for endpoint concerns.** It runs for every request,
   including ones that will 404, and it cannot see bound arguments.
2. **Hard-coding argument indexes in filters.** `GetArgument<T>(0)` breaks the
   moment somebody adds a `CancellationToken` in front of it. Search
   `context.Arguments` by type, or use a factory that resolves the index once at
   startup.
3. **Constraints as validation.** `{quantity:min(1)}` turns a bad request into a
   404 with no message.
4. **Expecting declaration order to break ties.** It does not; equal precedence
   is an ambiguity exception.
5. **`Results.Ok` in a union position.** It does not compile, and the fix is not
   to widen the return type to `IResult` — that throws away the metadata.
6. **Assuming a group filter can be cancelled per endpoint.** It cannot. Move the
   endpoint out of the group, or make the filter check metadata.
7. **Forgetting that a short circuit still unwinds outer filters.** Logging in an
   outer filter's tail will run even when an inner filter refused the request.

## 8. The interview answer

> *"When would you use an endpoint filter instead of middleware?"*

When the logic needs to know which endpoint it is running for, or needs the bound
arguments, or should not run for requests that will not reach a handler.
Middleware sits in front of routing and sees an unparsed request; an endpoint
filter sits between binding and the handler, sees the typed arguments and the
returned result, and is attached to a specific endpoint or group. Concretely:
correlation-id propagation and response compression are middleware; per-endpoint
validation, idempotency keys and result rewriting are filters. And filters can
short-circuit by returning an `IResult` without calling `next`, which reads far
better than writing to the response stream by hand.

## 9. Check yourself

1. What object does `MapGet` return, and when do its conventions actually run?
2. Two routes, `/bikes/{id:int}` and `/bikes/available`, declared in that order.
   Which handles `GET /bikes/available`? Why?
3. What status does `GET /bikes/abc` produce when only `/bikes/{id:int}` is
   registered, and why is that sometimes the wrong answer?
4. Give the exact execution order for a group filter, two endpoint filters and a
   handler, on the way in and on the way out.
5. What is the return type of `IEndpointFilter.InvokeAsync`, and what does
   returning without calling `next` do?
6. Why can a filter read the request body as a typed object while middleware
   cannot?
7. When does an `AddEndpointFilterFactory` lambda run, and what does returning
   `next` unchanged mean?
8. What does `Results<Ok<T>, NotFound>` give you that `IResult` does not?
9. Can a nested group remove a convention added by its parent? What is the
   idiomatic alternative?
10. Why is `GetArgument<T>(0)` fragile, and what is a safer way to reach the same
    argument?
11. Where does an exception thrown by a handler surface, relative to the filter
    chain?
12. What happens at runtime when two registered routes have identical
    precedence?

# Reading — how minimal APIs, groups and filters work underneath

## The problem the design is solving

ASP.NET Core has always had two request-processing concepts: middleware, which is
a chain around the whole application, and MVC filters, which are a chain around a
single action. Middleware is general and blind — it runs before routing has
picked a destination, so it knows the path but not the endpoint. MVC filters are
specific and sighted, but they came bundled with the whole MVC stack: a
controller type, an action selector, model binding conventions, action results.

Minimal APIs, shipped in .NET 6, kept the routing and dropped the stack. That was
a real gain in startup cost and in how much you had to know to write one
endpoint, but the first release lost something: there was no way to say "these
twelve endpoints share this behaviour" without writing an extension method that
each one had to remember to call. .NET 7 filled the gap with `MapGroup` and
`AddEndpointFilter`, and that is the version of minimal APIs worth learning.

## Endpoints as data

The unifying idea is that an endpoint is a value, not a piece of code. Routing
builds an immutable list of `Endpoint` objects from one or more
`EndpointDataSource`s. The `EndpointRoutingMiddleware` matches the incoming
request against a prebuilt matcher — a `DfaMatcher`, a deterministic finite
automaton compiled from the route templates at startup — and sets the selected
endpoint on `HttpContext.Features`. `EndpointMiddleware`, at the end of the
pipeline, invokes it.

Everything between those two points is middleware that reads *metadata* off the
selected endpoint. Authorization looks for `IAuthorizeData`. CORS looks for
`ICorsMetadata`. Output caching looks for its own policy metadata. Your own
middleware can do exactly the same:

```csharp
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    var endpoint = context.GetEndpoint();
    if (endpoint?.Metadata.GetMetadata<AuditMetadata>() is { } audit)
    {
        // this endpoint asked to be audited
    }
    await next(context);
});
```

That pattern — attach metadata at map time, read it in middleware — is how the
framework's own features are built, and it is available to you. It is also the
correct answer when a group convention needs an opt-out: publish a metadata
marker, and have the convention honour it, exactly as `AllowAnonymous` does.

## The DFA matcher, and why precedence is not order

Route matching is not a loop over templates. At startup the router builds a
`DfaMatcher`: a state machine keyed on path segments, where each state holds the
candidate endpoints reachable from it. Matching a path walks the automaton once,
segment by segment, which is why an application with two thousand routes matches
in roughly the time one with twenty does.

Candidates surviving the walk are ordered by *precedence*, computed per segment
at build time from the segment's kind — literal, constrained parameter,
parameter, catch-all — and then by explicit `Order`. Declaration order never
enters the calculation. When two candidates tie completely, the matcher throws
`AmbiguousMatchException`, because silently preferring one would make the routing
table dependent on file ordering.

The performance note that follows: constraints run during matching, on candidate
segments, so an expensive custom constraint is on the hot path for every request
that reaches that shape. `IRouteConstraint` implementations should be cheap and
allocation-free. A regex constraint compiles once and is fine; a constraint that
hits a database is a design error.

## Filters, folded once

The filter pipeline is built at startup by folding registrations right to left:

```
handler
  wrapped by endpoint filter 2
    wrapped by endpoint filter 1
      wrapped by group filter
```

Each `AddEndpointFilter` registration is really a factory —
`Func<EndpointFilterFactoryContext, EndpointFilterDelegate, EndpointFilterDelegate>` —
and `AddEndpointFilter<T>` is sugar that resolves `T` from DI (via
`ActivatorUtilities`, so constructor parameters come from the container) and
wraps it. `AddEndpointFilterFactory` exposes the raw form, which is why it is the
only variant that can look at `MethodInfo` and decline to wrap.

The per-request cost is one `EndpointFilterInvocationContext` allocation plus one
delegate invocation per filter. For handlers with up to a few parameters the
runtime uses a generic `DefaultEndpointFilterInvocationContext<T0, T1, ...>` to
avoid boxing the argument list; beyond that it falls back to an object array.
This is small, but it is not free: a filter added to a group of eighty endpoints
runs eighty times as often as you probably pictured when you wrote it.

Exceptions propagate outward through the chain like any other await, which makes
`try`/`catch` around `await next(context)` a legitimate scoped error handler. It
is deliberately *not* the same as `UseExceptionHandler`, which catches everything
including failures in middleware that ran before routing.

## Where the argument list comes from

Minimal API parameter binding is source-generated at build where possible and
reflection-emitted otherwise; either way the result is a `RequestDelegate` that
constructs each parameter from a known source — route values, query string,
headers, the JSON body, the DI container, or a well-known type such as
`HttpContext`, `ClaimsPrincipal` or `CancellationToken`. The bound values are
placed into the filter invocation context *in declaration order* before the first
filter runs.

That ordering is the whole reason `GetArgument<T>(index)` is positional, and the
whole reason it is fragile. The robust pattern in a hand-written filter is to
search by type:

```csharp
var ride = context.Arguments.OfType<RideRequest>().FirstOrDefault();
```

and the robust pattern in a factory is to compute the index once, at startup,
from `context.MethodInfo.GetParameters()`, and close over it.

## When not to use these tools

**Do not use an endpoint filter for something that must run before routing.**
Request logging that should also cover 404s, header normalisation, HTTPS
redirection, rate limiting that must reject before you spend work on matching —
all middleware.

**Do not use a group as a code-organisation device only.** A group is a
behavioural statement. If the endpoints share a URL prefix but nothing else, a
group with no conventions is fine; the smell is a group whose conventions apply
awkwardly to half its members, which usually means the URL shape and the policy
shape disagree and the URL shape won.

**Do not reach for minimal APIs when you need the MVC machinery.** Model-bound
complex forms, content negotiation across several formatters, view rendering,
`[ApiController]`'s automatic 400s and per-action attribute filters are all real
features that controllers give you for free. Minimal APIs deliberately do not
have content negotiation: they serialise to JSON, and an `Accept: application/xml`
header is ignored rather than honoured. If an existing controller-based API is
working, "port it to minimal APIs" is rarely a project with a payoff.

**Do not put policy in route constraints.** They are a matching optimisation.
Validation belongs where it can produce a message.

## Historical note

The `Results<T1, ...>` union types deserve a footnote. C# has no discriminated
unions, so the framework generates a family of generic structs implementing
`IResult` with implicit conversions from each member type, plus
`IEndpointMetadataProvider` so each member can contribute its own status code to
the OpenAPI document. It is a workaround that lands surprisingly well: you get
compile-time exhaustiveness over the *declared* set, and self-documenting
endpoints, at the cost of a fairly noisy signature. When the union grows past
three or four members, that noise is a signal — an endpoint with six outcomes is
usually two endpoints.

## Further reading

- [Minimal APIs quick reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis)
- [Filters in minimal API apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/min-api-filters)
- [Routing: route constraints](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/routing#route-constraint-reference)
- [Parameter binding in minimal APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/parameter-binding)
- [Endpoint metadata and `IEndpointMetadataProvider`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/responses)
