## Exercise 1 — one group, two endpoints, one shared decision

Edit `src/Api/V3DA01_MinimalApis/Ex1.cs`. The depot data is given at the bottom
of the file: three docks (`kings`, `wharf`, `mile`) and five bikes.

Build a single group at `/v3da01/docks`, tagged `v3da01`, and map two endpoints
into it:

- `GET /v3da01/docks` — every dock as `{"id","name","capacity"}`, ordered by
  `id` ascending (ordinal string comparison):

```json
[{"id":"kings","name":"Kings Cross","capacity":30},
 {"id":"mile","name":"Mile End","capacity":12},
 {"id":"wharf","name":"Canary Wharf","capacity":24}]
```

- `GET /v3da01/docks/{id}` — that dock, or **404** with no body when the id is
  unknown. Ids are compared case-sensitively, so `/v3da01/docks/Kings` is a 404.

Both the prefix and the tag must be declared **once**, on the group. Mapping the
two routes with their full paths and two `WithTags` calls passes nothing.

Watch the second path. Inside a group, `MapGet("/{id}")` gives
`/v3da01/docks/{id}`; `MapGet("docks/{id}")` gives `/v3da01/docks/docks/{id}`,
which is a route that exists and is not the one you wanted.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da01_minimal_api_groups ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A group is a value, not a syntax. `app.MapGroup("/v3da01/docks")` hands you back
an object that is itself an `IEndpointRouteBuilder`, so the two `MapGet` calls go
on *that*, not on `app`.

## Hint 2

The same idea for a different resource:

    var lockers = app.MapGroup("/depot/lockers").WithTags("depot");
    lockers.MapGet("/", () => TypedResults.Ok(All()));
    lockers.MapGet("/{code}", (string code) => Find(code) is { } l
        ? Results<Ok<Locker>, NotFound>.op_Implicit(TypedResults.Ok(l))
        : TypedResults.NotFound());

You do not need the union here — plain `IResult` is fine for ex1.

## Hint 3

`ListDocks` projects `V3DA01Depot.Docks` into `DockDto`, ordered with
`OrderBy(d => d.Id, StringComparer.Ordinal)`. `GetDock` looks the dock up and
returns `TypedResults.NotFound()` when it is missing. The decision left to you is
whether the group prefix ends in a slash — try it both ways and read the failing
path in the gate output.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the wire, not the code. The gate issues exactly three requests:
`GET /v3da01/docks`, `GET /v3da01/docks/kings` and `GET /v3da01/docks/Kings`. If
any of them 404s when it should not, your route *text* is wrong, not your logic.

## Hint 2

The commonest failure is a doubled segment. Print your route table at startup and
look at it:

    foreach (var source in app.Services
        .GetRequiredService<EndpointDataSource>().Endpoints)
    {
        Console.WriteLine(source.DisplayName);
    }

## Hint 3

Ordering is graded ordinally, not culture-sensitively. `OrderBy(d => d.Id)` uses
the current culture's comparer, which happens to agree here but will not always;
pass `StringComparer.Ordinal` and mean it. The lookup for a single dock must be
case-sensitive for the same reason — `FirstOrDefault(d => d.Id == id)` already
is.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — precedence, and the 404 that is really a 400

Edit `src/Api/V3DA01_MinimalApis/Ex2.cs`. Map three routes that all live under
`/v3da01/bikes/` and all match a single segment. Declare them **in this order**,
which is deliberately the wrong order if declaration order mattered:

1. `GET /v3da01/bikes/{id:int}` — the bike with that id as
   `{"id","dockId","state"}`, or **404** when there is no such bike.
2. `GET /v3da01/bikes/{dockId:alpha}` — every bike at that dock, id ascending, or
   **404** when the dock is unknown.
3. `GET /v3da01/bikes/available` — every bike whose `state` is `ready`, id
   ascending.

Expected:

- `GET /v3da01/bikes/3` → 200 `{"id":3,"dockId":"wharf","state":"ready"}`
- `GET /v3da01/bikes/wharf` → 200 with bikes 3 and 5
- `GET /v3da01/bikes/available` → 200 with bikes 1, 3, 5 — the **literal wins**
  over the `alpha` parameter even though it was declared last
- `GET /v3da01/bikes/9x` → **404**, because `9x` is neither an `int` nor `alpha`,
  so no candidate survived matching

Also map `GET /v3da01/bikes/by-id?id={id}`, which does the same job as route 1
but binds `id` from the query string as a `string`, and answers **400** with a
validation problem keyed `"id"` when the value does not parse as an integer:

```json
{"errors":{"id":["Not an integer."]}}
```

That pair is the point of the exercise. Route 1 and `by-id` fail differently on
the same bad input, and only one of them tells the client what went wrong.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da01_minimal_api_groups ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are not being asked to order anything. The router computes precedence per
segment at startup — literal, then constrained parameter, then bare parameter —
and declaration order never enters it. Write the three routes in the order given
and let the matcher be right.

## Hint 2

Two constrained parameters in the same position do not collide when their
constraints are disjoint:

    app.MapGet("/warehouse/{bay:int}", ByBay);
    app.MapGet("/warehouse/{aisle:alpha}", ByAisle);

`/warehouse/12` reaches `ByBay`, `/warehouse/east` reaches `ByAisle`, and
`/warehouse/12east` reaches neither. Candidates that fail a constraint are
eliminated before ambiguity is even considered.

## Hint 3

For `by-id`, bind `string? id` and use `int.TryParse`. Return
`TypedResults.ValidationProblem(new Dictionary<string, string[]> { ["id"] =
["Not an integer."] })` when it fails. The decision left to you: what should
`by-id` do when `id` is absent entirely? Pick an answer you can defend, then
check it against the gate.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Predict before you run. Write down, for each of `/3`, `/wharf`, `/available`,
`/9x`, which of your three routes you expect to match and what status you expect.
Then run the gate. Every disagreement is a precedence rule you have not
internalised yet.

## Hint 2

If you get an `AmbiguousMatchException` at request time, two of your routes have
identical precedence for the path being requested — which means you dropped a
constraint. `{dockId}` and `{id:int}` *do* collide on `/3`; `{dockId:alpha}` and
`{id:int}` do not.

## Hint 3

The `by-id` half is the argument the exercise is really making. A constraint is a
matching device: when it rejects, the client is told the resource does not exist,
which is a lie about a malformed identifier. Bind the value, parse it yourself,
and you can answer 400 with the field name in it. Use constraints to
disambiguate routes; use code to validate input.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — your first filter, and the header you can still set afterwards

Edit `src/Api/V3DA01_MinimalApis/Ex3.cs`. Map a group at `/v3da01/audit` with one
endpoint, `GET /v3da01/audit/docks`, returning the dock count:

```json
{"count":3}
```

Add **one** endpoint filter to the group, as an inline lambda, that:

- before calling `next`, sets the response header `X-Depot-Filter` to `v3da01`;
- after `next` returns, sets the response header `X-Depot-Result` to the CLR type
  name of the returned object — `Ok<DockCount>` for this endpoint.

So the response carries both headers *and* the JSON body. That combination is the
lesson: the object your filter returns has not been executed yet, so the response
has not started, so writing a header after `await next(context)` still reaches the
client. Try the same thing in middleware after `await next()` and you get an
`InvalidOperationException` about headers being read-only, because by then the
response has been sent.

Expected response headers on `GET /v3da01/audit/docks`:

```
X-Depot-Filter: v3da01
X-Depot-Result: Ok`1
```

Use `result?.GetType().Name`, which for `Ok<DockCount>` is the backtick-arity
name `Ok`1`. Do not prettify it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da01_minimal_api_groups ex3
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what "the response has started" means. A minimal API handler returns an
`IResult`; nothing has been written to the socket yet. The framework executes
that result *after* the whole filter chain unwinds. Everything about this
exercise follows from that one fact.

## Hint 2

If you see `System.InvalidOperationException: Headers are read-only, response has
already started`, you are writing to the response after something has flushed it —
which in a filter means you executed the result yourself, or you wrote to
`Response.Body` directly. Do neither; return the result and let the framework run
it.

## Hint 3

`X-Depot-Result` is `Ok`1` and not `Ok<DockCount>` because `Type.Name` gives the
CLR metadata name, where generic arity is a backtick and a digit. If you find
yourself reaching for `ToString()` on the type to make it prettier, stop — the
gate compares the raw name, and the raw name is what a log line would carry.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — refusing the request without calling the handler

Edit `src/Api/V3DA01_MinimalApis/Ex4.cs`. Map a group at `/v3da01/keyed` with one
endpoint, `POST /v3da01/keyed/checks`, whose handler is given and returns 200
`{"ok":true}` — and which the gate asserts is **never entered** when the key is
wrong (it increments `Ex4.HandlerCalls`, which the gate reads back through
`GET /v3da01/keyed/calls`).

Add a group filter that inspects the `X-Depot-Key` request header:

- header absent or empty → **400**, `application/problem+json`, with
  `title` = `Missing depot key` and `status` = 400
- header present but not `v3da01-key` → **403**, `application/problem+json`, with
  `title` = `Unknown depot key` and `status` = 403
- header exactly `v3da01-key` → the handler runs, 200 `{"ok":true}`

`GET /v3da01/keyed/calls` is mapped **outside** the group and returns
`{"calls":n}`; it must not require the key. That is the second half of the point:
a filter attached to a group is not a global gate, and moving one endpoint out of
the group is how you exempt it.

Sequence the gate runs: two bad requests, then one good one, then
`GET /v3da01/keyed/calls`, expecting `{"calls":1}`.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da01_minimal_api_groups ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Short-circuiting is not a special API. It is `return` without `await next(...)`.
Whatever you return becomes the response.

## Hint 2

Reading a header and refusing, for a different header:

    if (!context.HttpContext.Request.Headers.TryGetValue("X-Trace", out var v)
        || StringValues.IsNullOrEmpty(v))
    {
        return TypedResults.Problem(title: "Missing trace header", statusCode: 400);
    }

`TypedResults.Problem` writes `application/problem+json` for you, with `title`,
`status` and a `traceId`.

## Hint 3

Two guards, then `return await next(context);`. The decision left to you is the
status codes: the prompt fixes them at 400 and 403, but be able to say why a
missing key is a malformed request and a wrong key is a refused one — and why
neither of them is a 401 here, given that no authentication scheme is involved.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Work backwards from `HandlerCalls`. The counter exists so the gate can prove the
handler was skipped rather than merely that the status was 400. Any solution that
validates inside the handler will produce the right status codes and still fail.

## Hint 2

Check the content type on the failures. A bare `Results.BadRequest("...")` gives
you `text/plain` and no `title` field; the gate parses the body as problem+json.
`TypedResults.Problem(title: ..., statusCode: ...)` is the one that produces:

    {"type":"...","title":"Missing depot key","status":400,"traceId":"..."}

## Hint 3

`/v3da01/keyed/calls` sharing a prefix with the group does not put it in the
group. `app.MapGet("/v3da01/keyed/calls", ...)` maps it on the application, so
the group's conventions never touch it. There is no way to unsubscribe an
endpoint from a group it was mapped into — the exemption has to be a mapping
decision.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — proving the order instead of remembering it

Edit `src/Api/V3DA01_MinimalApis/Ex5.cs`. Map a group at `/v3da01/order` carrying
one filter named `g1`, and inside it one endpoint, `GET /v3da01/order/trace`,
carrying two filters named `e1` and `e2` — added in that order.

Every filter appends to a `List<string>` kept in `HttpContext.Items["v3da01"]`:
`"<name>>"` before calling `next`, `"<name><"` after it returns. The handler
appends `"handler"` and returns 200 `{"ok":true}`.

The **outermost** filter, `g1`, appends its own closing token and then writes the
whole list, joined with `,`, to the response header `X-Filter-Trace`. Expected:

```
X-Filter-Trace: g1>,e1>,e2>,handler,e2<,e1<,g1<
```

Two things to take from the result. Group conventions are applied before endpoint
conventions, so the group filter is *outermost*, not innermost — the opposite of
what "more specific wins" would suggest. And the unwind is exact mirror order,
because each filter is simply resuming after its own `await`.

Then add a second endpoint to the same group, `GET /v3da01/order/plain`, with no
endpoint filters of its own. Its trace must be `g1>,handler,g1<` — a group filter
runs for every member of the group and only for members of the group.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da01_minimal_api_groups ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are building one list per request, shared by four pieces of code that cannot
see each other. `HttpContext.Items` is the per-request dictionary that exists for
exactly this.

## Hint 2

A helper keeps the four call sites honest:

    static List<string> Trace(HttpContext http) =>
        (List<string>)(http.Items["v3da01"] ??= new List<string>());

Then a filter body is `Trace(ctx.HttpContext).Add("e1>");` … `await next(ctx)` …
`Trace(ctx.HttpContext).Add("e1<");`.

## Hint 3

`g1` writes the header after appending `g1<`, so the header line contains the
complete trace including its own close. The decision left to you: `e1` and `e2`
are added with two separate `AddEndpointFilter` calls on the same
`RouteHandlerBuilder` — work out from the expected string which of those two
calls produces the *outer* one before you write them.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Guess the string first. Write `X-Filter-Trace:` and your predicted value on
paper, run the gate, and compare. Being wrong here is worth more than being
right, because the mistake is almost always "the endpoint filter must be
outermost, it is more specific" — and it is not.

## Hint 2

If your trace is missing the tail tokens for `e1` and `e2`, something short-
circuited: one of the filters returned without awaiting `next`. If the trace has
duplicated tokens, `Items` is being replaced rather than appended to — `??=`
assigns only when the slot is null.

## Hint 3

The `plain` endpoint is the control experiment. If its trace picks up `e1` or
`e2`, you added those filters to the *group* builder rather than to the value
returned by `MapGet`. `AddEndpointFilter` exists on both, returns the same
builder it was called on, and reads identically at the call site — which is why
this mistake is common and silent.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — a filter class, a dependency, and a bound argument

Edit `src/Api/V3DA01_MinimalApis/Ex6.cs`. `Ex6Services` must register a singleton
`V3DA01Limits` with `MaxMinutes = 120`, and the filter class must take it through
its constructor.

Write `RideRequestFilter : IEndpointFilter` and attach it with
`AddEndpointFilter<RideRequestFilter>()` to `POST /v3da01/rides`, whose handler
signature is:

```csharp
private static IResult StartRide(RideRequest body, CancellationToken cancellation)
```

`RideRequest` is `record RideRequest(int BikeId, int Minutes)`. The filter checks
the already-bound body and refuses before the handler:

- `Minutes` less than 1 or greater than `MaxMinutes` → **400** validation problem
  keyed `"minutes"`, message `Between 1 and 120 minutes.`
- no bike with `BikeId` → **404**, no body
- the bike's `state` is not `ready` → **409** problem, `title` = `Bike not
  available`
- otherwise the handler runs and returns **201** with
  `Location: /v3da01/rides/{bikeId}` and body `{"bikeId":n,"minutes":m}`

Check the order the gate asserts: a request with `minutes = 0` **and** an unknown
bike gets the 400. Shape errors before existence errors, because a request you
cannot parse is not a question about a resource.

Reach the argument by **type**, not by index — `context.Arguments.OfType<
RideRequest>().First()`. `GetArgument<RideRequest>(0)` also works today and
breaks the day somebody puts the `CancellationToken` first.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da01_minimal_api_groups ex6
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the failing case the gate cares about most: `{"bikeId":999,
"minutes":0}`. Two things are wrong with it and exactly one status is correct.
Decide the precedence rule first and the code writes itself.

## Hint 2

`InvalidCastException` from inside a filter, at request time, means the argument
list is not the shape you assumed. Print it once while you are developing:

    foreach (var a in context.Arguments) Console.WriteLine(a?.GetType().FullName);

You will see `RideRequest` and — depending on the framework version and the
handler signature — nothing at all for `CancellationToken`, which is precisely
why index-based access is a trap.

## Hint 3

A 409 needs a body the client can read. `TypedResults.Problem(title: "Bike not
available", statusCode: 409)` gives problem+json; `TypedResults.Conflict()` gives
an empty 409 that tells nobody anything. The gate reads `title`, so the choice is
forced here — but notice that it is forced by the client's needs, not by the
framework.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — a return type the compiler and the document both believe

Edit `src/Api/V3DA01_MinimalApis/Ex7.cs`. Map `GET /v3da01/typed/bikes/{id}` —
note the **unconstrained** `{id}` — with this exact signature:

```csharp
private static Results<Ok<BikeDto>, NotFound, ValidationProblem> GetBike(string id)
```

Behaviour:

- `id` does not parse as an integer → **400** validation problem keyed `"id"`,
  message `Not an integer.`
- parses, but no such bike → **404**, empty body
- otherwise → **200** with the `BikeDto`

Then map `GET /v3da01/typed/metadata`, which reports what the framework knows
about the first endpoint *without* you telling it. Resolve
`EndpointDataSource` from DI, find the endpoint whose display name contains
`/v3da01/typed/bikes`, read every `IProducesResponseTypeMetadata` off its
metadata collection, and return the distinct status codes ascending:

```json
{"statusCodes":[200,400,404]}
```

You will not write a single `Produces` call. The union type implements
`IEndpointMetadataProvider`, and each member contributes its own status code at
build time. Change the signature to plain `IResult` and that array comes back
empty — which is the argument for unions in one experiment.

Return `TypedResults.Ok(...)`, not `Results.Ok(...)`: the former is typed
`Ok<BikeDto>` and converts implicitly into the union, the latter is `IResult` and
will not compile.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da01_minimal_api_groups ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Results<A, B, C>` is a struct with implicit conversions from each of `A`, `B`
and `C`. You never name it in the method body — you just `return
TypedResults.NotFound();` and the conversion happens.

## Hint 2

Reading endpoint metadata, for a different piece of it:

    var source = http.RequestServices.GetRequiredService<EndpointDataSource>();
    var endpoint = source.Endpoints
        .First(e => e.DisplayName!.Contains("/depot/lockers"));
    var tags = endpoint.Metadata.GetMetadata<ITagsMetadata>()?.Tags ?? [];

`GetOrderedMetadata<T>()` gives you every match rather than the last one, which
is what you want when several pieces of metadata share an interface.

## Hint 3

`endpoint.Metadata.GetOrderedMetadata<IProducesResponseTypeMetadata>()`, select
`StatusCode`, `Distinct()`, `Order()`, `ToList()`. The decision left to you:
`RouteEndpoint` versus `Endpoint` when you filter the data source — you can get
the route template off the former, which is a sturdier match than a display-name
substring.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Do the destructive experiment first. Write the endpoint returning `IResult`, hit
`/v3da01/typed/metadata`, and watch it return `{"statusCodes":[]}`. Then change
the signature to the union and watch three numbers appear. Now you know exactly
what the union buys.

## Hint 2

`Cannot implicitly convert type 'Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.IResult' to
'Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.HttpResults.Results<...>'` means you used
`Results.Ok`. `Results` (plural, static) makes `IResult`; `TypedResults` makes
concrete types. The union only accepts the concrete ones.

## Hint 3

The metadata endpoint must not find *itself*. If your filter is a substring match
on `bikes`, and you later add another bikes route, the `First` call starts
returning something else. Match on the route pattern's `RawText` — it is exact,
and it is what the router itself matched on.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the factory decides at startup which endpoints to wrap

Edit `src/Api/V3DA01_MinimalApis/Ex8.cs`. Map a group at `/v3da01/factory` with
two endpoints:

- `POST /v3da01/factory/rides` — handler takes `(RideRequest body)` and returns
  201 `{"bikeId":n,"minutes":m}`
- `GET /v3da01/factory/rides/{id:int}` — handler takes `(int id)` and returns 200
  `{"bikeId":id,"minutes":30}`

Add **one** `AddEndpointFilterFactory` to the group. The factory must:

1. look through `context.MethodInfo.GetParameters()` for a parameter of type
   `RideRequest`;
2. if there is none, `return next` unchanged — that endpoint gets no filter at
   all, not a filter that does nothing;
3. if there is one, capture its **index** in a local and return a filter that
   reads `context.GetArgument<RideRequest>(index)`, sets the response header
   `X-Ride-Checked` to `true`, and refuses `Minutes < 1` with a **400**
   validation problem keyed `"minutes"`.

Expected:

- `POST /v3da01/factory/rides` with `{"bikeId":1,"minutes":30}` → 201, header
  `X-Ride-Checked: true`
- `POST` with `{"bikeId":1,"minutes":0}` → 400, header present, body has
  `errors.minutes`
- `GET /v3da01/factory/rides/7` → 200, and **no** `X-Ride-Checked` header at all

The index is computed once, at startup, and closed over. That is the difference
between a factory and a plain filter: the reflection happens while the
application is being built, and the per-request path is an array index. Doing
`GetParameters()` inside the per-request delegate would work and would be a
measurable mistake on a hot endpoint.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da01_minimal_api_groups ex8
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The `GET` endpoint is the assertion that matters. Anything that "wraps everything
and returns early for the wrong shape" produces correct statuses and still fails,
because the header would be missing but the filter would still be in the chain —
and the next reader would believe reflection runs per request.

## Hint 2

If both endpoints get the header, your factory returned a filter unconditionally.
If neither does, `context.MethodInfo` is not seeing what you expect: it is the
`MethodInfo` of the *handler delegate*, so a lambda handler gives you a compiler-
generated method whose parameters are still the ones you declared. Method groups
and lambdas both work here.

## Hint 3

`GetArgument<T>(index)` is safe in this one situation — the index came from the
same `MethodInfo` the arguments were built from, at the same moment, and both are
frozen for the life of the application. That is the general rule for positional
access: it is fine when the position was derived, and a bug when it was typed.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — nested groups, a built filter, and an idempotent write

Honest difficulty note: the idempotency store is a dictionary and four lines. The
part that catches people is deciding where in the chain the replay check belongs,
and what a replayed response is allowed to look like.

Edit `src/Api/V3DA01_MinimalApis/Challenge.cs`. Build two nested groups:

- outer: `/v3da01/ops`, carrying the `X-Depot-Key` filter from ex4 (missing →
  400 `Missing depot key`, wrong → 403 `Unknown depot key`)
- inner: `/v3da01/ops/rides`, carrying an idempotency filter added through
  `AddEndpointFilterFactory` — built **only** for endpoints whose `MethodInfo`
  declares a `RideRequest` parameter

Map two endpoints into the inner group:

- `POST /v3da01/ops/rides`, signature
  `Results<Created<RideDto>, ValidationProblem, ProblemHttpResult> StartRide(RideRequest body)`
- `GET /v3da01/ops/rides/count`, returning `{"count":n}` where `n` is the number
  of distinct rides actually created

The idempotency filter:

1. reads `X-Idempotency-Key`; absent or empty → **400** problem, `title` =
   `Missing idempotency key`
2. if that key has been seen before, return the **stored** `RideDto` as a **200**
   (not a 201) with header `X-Idempotent-Replay: true`, without calling `next`
3. otherwise call `next`; if the result is a `Created<RideDto>`, store its value
   under the key before returning it

Validation stays in the handler: `Minutes` outside 1..120 → 400 keyed
`"minutes"`; unknown `BikeId` → 404 via `TypedResults.Problem(title: "No such
bike", statusCode: 404)`.

The gate's sequence, all with a valid depot key:

1. `POST` `{"bikeId":1,"minutes":30}` with key `k1` → **201**, `Location:
   /v3da01/ops/rides/1`, no replay header
2. the identical request again with key `k1` → **200**, same body, header
   `X-Idempotent-Replay: true`
3. `POST` `{"bikeId":1,"minutes":0}` with key `k2` → **400** keyed `"minutes"`,
   and `k2` is **not** stored
4. the same bad request again with key `k2` → **400** again, no replay header
5. `POST` with no `X-Idempotency-Key` → **400** `Missing idempotency key`
6. `POST` with no `X-Depot-Key` → **400** `Missing depot key`, and the
   idempotency filter never runs
7. `GET /v3da01/ops/rides/count` → `{"count":1}`

Step 3 and 4 together are the design decision: only *successful* results are
recorded, so a client that fixes its payload and retries with the same key gets
the fixed behaviour rather than a cached rejection.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da01_minimal_api_groups challenge
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Read the gate sequence as a state machine over the store. After step 1 it has one
entry; after step 3 it still has one entry; after step 7 the count endpoint must
agree. Any solution that stores on the way *in* rather than on the way out fails
step 4.

## Hint 2

If step 6 produces `Missing idempotency key` instead of `Missing depot key`, your
filters are nested the wrong way round — you attached the depot-key filter to the
inner group, or the idempotency filter to the outer one. Group conventions run
outermost-first, and the outer group is the one whose `MapGroup` was called on
`app`.

## Hint 3

`GET /v3da01/ops/rides/count` has no `RideRequest` parameter, so the factory
returns `next` and the count endpoint needs no idempotency key — but it is still
inside the outer group, so it *does* need a depot key. Confirm both halves; a
factory that wraps everything makes the count endpoint demand a key nobody would
think to send.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — the filter as a scoped exception handler

`review1` is not part of finishing this sector; the scheduler brings it back
later.

Edit `src/Api/V3DA01_MinimalApis/Review1.cs`. The domain code is given and
throws:

```csharp
public class UnknownDockException(string dockId) : Exception($"No dock {dockId}.")
{
    public string DockId { get; } = dockId;
}

public class DockFullException(string dockId, int capacity) : Exception("Dock full.")
{
    public string DockId { get; } = dockId;
    public int Capacity { get; } = capacity;
}
```

Map `POST /v3da01/review/docks/{dockId}/bikes` with body `{"bikeId":n}`. The
handler is given and calls `V3DA01Review.Park(dockId, bikeId)`, which throws
`UnknownDockException` for an unknown dock, `DockFullException` when the dock is
at capacity, and otherwise returns a `BikeDto`. **Do not edit the handler and do
not catch anything inside it.**

Add one endpoint filter that wraps `await next(context)` in a `try`/`catch` and
translates:

- `UnknownDockException` → **404** problem, `title` = `No such dock`, and an
  extension member `dockId` carrying the id
- `DockFullException` → **409** problem, `title` = `Dock full`, extension members
  `dockId` and `capacity`
- anything else → rethrow, untouched

Success is **201** with `Location: /v3da01/review/docks/{dockId}/bikes/{bikeId}`.

The `mile` dock has capacity 12 and the review store starts it with 12 bikes
parked, so `POST /v3da01/review/docks/mile/bikes` is your 409, `kings` is your
201 and `nowhere` is your 404.

Two things to be able to say afterwards. Why this belongs in a filter rather than
in `UseExceptionHandler`: the translation knows about *these* endpoints' domain
exceptions, and a global handler that knew about every module's exceptions would
be a dependency magnet. And why the `catch` works at all: a filter is just an
`await` in the call chain, so an exception from the handler unwinds outward
through every filter that has not returned yet.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da01_minimal_api_groups review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You have written `try { await next(context); }` shaped code before — it is a
`using` block turned inside out. The filter is the only place in this chain that
knows both the domain exceptions and the HTTP vocabulary, which is why the
translation lives there.

## Hint 2

Extension members go into the `extensions` dictionary:

    return TypedResults.Problem(
        title: "No such bay",
        statusCode: 404,
        extensions: new Dictionary<string, object?> { ["bayId"] = ex.BayId });

They are serialised as top-level members of the problem document, alongside
`type`, `title` and `status` — that is what RFC 9457 means by an extension.

## Hint 3

Two `catch` clauses, most specific first, and no `catch (Exception)` at the end.
The decision left to you: filter on the endpoint or on a group? There is one
endpoint here, but write the version you would want when there are nine, and be
able to say what happens to an unrelated `NullReferenceException` under your
answer.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from what the client sees. A 500 with a stack trace and a 409 with
`{"title":"Dock full","dockId":"mile","capacity":12}` are the same event; only
one of them lets the caller do something about it. Everything in this exercise is
in service of the second.

## Hint 2

If your 409 body has no `capacity` member, you passed the extensions to the wrong
parameter or built a plain anonymous object. `TypedResults.Problem` takes
`extensions` as `IDictionary<string, object?>`; anything you put there appears at
the top level of the document, and anything you put in `detail` appears as a
string.

## Hint 3

Rethrowing matters. `catch (Exception) { return TypedResults.Problem(...); }`
would swallow a genuine bug into a tidy 500 and lose the stack trace — and with
`throw ex;` instead of `throw;` you lose it even when you meant to keep it. Catch
only the two exceptions you can translate and let the rest travel; the developer
exception page and your logging both need them intact.

lessons.title: V3·DA2 — Model binding, validation and problem details
lessons.summary: Binding is the layer that turns an HTTP request into method arguments, and it fails in ways your handler never sees. This sector covers where each parameter comes from, how to teach the binder your own types, and how to answer a bad request with a problem document a client can actually act on.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·DA2 — Model binding, validation and problem details

The previous sector left you with endpoints whose parameters simply appeared:
`GetDock(string id)` got its id, `StartRide(RideRequest body)` got its body, and
nothing in between was visible. This sector opens that box, because the space
between "an HTTP request arrived" and "your method was called with these
arguments" is where a surprising share of production bugs live — and where the
difference between an API that is pleasant to integrate against and one that is
not is almost entirely decided.

Consider a request that should fail. A customs declaration arrives with a tariff
code of `99`, a `quantity` of `-4`, a `Content-Type` of `text/plain`, and a
trailing comma in the JSON. Four different failures, at four different layers,
and by default your API answers three of them with responses that tell the client
nothing useful and the fourth with a 500. The purpose of this sector is that all
four should be a well-formed problem document naming the thing that was wrong.

## Concept — binding is a set of rules, not magic

For each parameter of your handler, the framework picks a **source**, once, at
build time. In order of how it decides:

1. Is there an explicit attribute — `[FromRoute]`, `[FromQuery]`, `[FromHeader]`,
   `[FromBody]`, `[FromForm]`, `[FromServices]`, `[AsParameters]`? Then that.
2. Is it a special type — `HttpContext`, `HttpRequest`, `ClaimsPrincipal`,
   `CancellationToken`, `IFormFileCollection`, `Stream`? Then that.
3. Does the parameter name match a **route parameter** in the pattern? Then route.
4. Is the type a "simple" type — one with a `TryParse`, or a string? Then query.
5. Does the type define a static `BindAsync`? Then that, from the whole request.
6. Is the type registered in DI? Then services.
7. Otherwise: the **body**, deserialised as JSON.

Two of those steps deserve a warning label. Step 3 matches on **name**, so
renaming a route parameter from `{id}` to `{dockId}` while leaving the handler
parameter called `id` silently changes it from a route binding to a query
binding, and your handler starts receiving null. And step 7 is a fallback, which
means a typo in a type name or a missing DI registration ends up being read as a
request body — producing an error message about JSON when the real problem was a
registration.

## Concept — three different failures wear the same status code

Once binding has a source, it has to produce a value, and there are three ways
that goes wrong. They are worth separating in your head because they surface
differently:

**The value cannot be parsed.** `?quantity=lots` for an `int quantity`. The
framework short-circuits with a **400** before your handler runs, and — this is
the part that stings — with an empty body by default. The client sees a bare 400
and has to guess which of its fields the API disliked.

**The body cannot be deserialised.** Malformed JSON, or a `Content-Type` that is
not JSON. Malformed JSON is a 400; the wrong content type is a **415 Unsupported
Media Type**. Both are produced by the framework before your code runs.

**The value parsed fine and is nonsense.** `quantity: -4`. Nothing has failed
technically; the binder did its job. This one is yours, and it is the only one of
the three where you get to choose the status code, the message and the shape.

Knowing which layer produced a given 400 is the difference between a five-minute
fix and an afternoon.

## Concept — the problem document

RFC 7807, revised as RFC 9457, defines a small JSON object for machine-readable
errors:

```json
{
  "type": "https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc9110#section-15.5.1",
  "title": "One or more validation errors occurred.",
  "status": 400,
  "traceId": "00-8f2a...-01",
  "errors": { "quantity": ["Must be positive."] }
}
```

`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance` are the defined members;
anything else — `traceId`, `errors`, your own `declarationId` — is an
**extension**, and extensions are explicitly allowed. The content type is
`application/problem+json`, not `application/json`, and a client that checks it
can route the body to an error parser without guessing.

ASP.NET Core gives you three ways in. `TypedResults.Problem(...)` and
`TypedResults.ValidationProblem(...)` build one by hand.
`builder.Services.AddProblemDetails()` registers an `IProblemDetailsService` and
makes the framework produce problem documents for status-code-only responses that
would otherwise have empty bodies. And `CustomizeProblemDetails` is a hook that
runs over every document the framework generates, which is where a `traceId` or
an environment marker belongs — written once rather than in ninety handlers.

## What this sector drills

The domain is a **customs declaration API** under `/v3da02/...`: declarations,
line items and tariff codes. Exercise 1 walks the binding sources explicitly.
Exercise 2 handles the query string's awkward shapes — repeated keys, arrays,
absent versus empty. Exercises 3 and 4 teach the binder your own types, first
with `TryParse` for a single value and then with `BindAsync` for a type assembled
from several headers. Exercise 5 collapses eight query parameters into one
`[AsParameters]` struct and validates it in one place.

Exercises 6, 7 and 8 are the error surface. Six separates deserialisation
failures from validation failures and gives each one an honest body. Seven builds
a real `ValidationProblemDetails` with several messages per field and settles the
400-versus-422 argument. Eight registers an `IExceptionHandler` so an escaped
domain exception becomes a 409 problem document rather than a 500.

The challenge is one write endpoint that does all of it. The review comes back at
the same ideas from the read side, where the interesting failures are headers and
content negotiation rather than bodies.

The habit worth forming: for every endpoint you write, name the four ways a
client can get it wrong and check what your API actually returns for each. Most
APIs answer at least one of them with a blank 400, and nobody notices until an
integrator asks.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/v3da02_binding_validation_problems

Binding and error shape are the two halves of an API's contract that nobody
writes down and every integrator discovers. These are the mechanisms.

## Notes

**Binding decisions are made once, at build time.** The minimal API
infrastructure generates a `RequestDelegate` per endpoint that knows each
parameter's source. It is not re-derived per request, and it is not affected by
what the client sends. A parameter bound from the query stays bound from the
query even when the same name appears in the route.

**Name matching against the route is the silent one.** Rule 3 — "the parameter
name matches a route parameter" — is case-insensitive and exact. Rename the
template segment and the parameter quietly falls through to the query-string
rule, where it will be null on every request and throw no error at all. If you
want that binding to be load-bearing, write `[FromRoute]` and let a mismatch
become a startup exception instead of a silent null.

**"Simple type" means `TryParse` exists.** The binder looks for a static
`TryParse(string, IFormatProvider, out T)` — the `IParsable<T>` shape — or the
older `TryParse(string, out T)`. Anything with one of those binds from a single
string: route, query or header. Anything without one, and without `BindAsync`,
falls through to the body.

**`BindAsync` sees the whole request.** Static
`ValueTask<T?> BindAsync(HttpContext, ParameterInfo)` on your type takes it out
of the single-string world entirely: read three headers, the route and a claim,
and return the assembled object — or `null`, which binds the parameter to null
rather than failing, so a required value needs its own check.

**Nullability decides required-ness for simple types.** `int quantity` with no
`?quantity=` is a 400 before your handler; `int? quantity` is null and your
problem. For the **body**, the rule is inverted in a way that catches everyone:
a body parameter is required by default, an empty body is a 400, and
`[FromBody(EmptyBodyBehavior = EmptyBodyBehavior.Allow)]` or a nullable parameter
type is how you opt out.

**Query strings have no arrays, only repeated keys.** `?code=1&code=2` produces
`StringValues` with two entries; `int[] codes` binds it. A single `?code=1` gives
a one-element array, and no `code=` at all gives an **empty** array rather than
null. `?code=` — present and empty — gives a one-element array containing the
empty string, which is a real source of off-by-one bugs in filters.

**`AddProblemDetails` fills empty bodies.** Without it,
`TypedResults.NotFound()` sends a 404 with no content. With it, the
`ProblemDetailsMiddleware` notices a 4xx/5xx status with no body and writes a
problem document. It does *not* rewrite bodies you produced yourself.

**`CustomizeProblemDetails` runs on everything the framework generates.** It is
the right home for `traceId`, `instance`, and stripping `detail` outside
Development. It is the wrong home for per-endpoint semantics, because it cannot
tell endpoints apart without digging metadata out of the `HttpContext`.

## ex1 - one endpoint, four sources

Writing `[FromRoute]`, `[FromQuery]`, `[FromHeader]` and `[FromBody]` explicitly,
even where the defaults would have picked the same source, is a readability
argument as much as a correctness one: the next reader does not have to run the
seven-step algorithm in their head. The case where it stops being cosmetic is the
header, where the parameter name and the header name almost never match —
`[FromHeader(Name = "X-Declarant")]` is the only way to bind `X-Declarant` to a
parameter called `declarant`.

## ex2 - the query string is a multimap

`int[]`, `StringValues` and `string?` over the same key behave differently, and
you measured all three. The distinction that matters in practice is **absent**
versus **present and empty**, because a filter built from the second silently
matches nothing. Bind `StringValues` when you need to tell them apart; bind an
array when you do not care.

## ex3 - TryParse makes a type bindable

Implementing `IParsable<TariffCode>` — `Parse` and `TryParse` — is enough for the
binder to accept `TariffCode` from a route or a query. The payoff is that
validation moves into the type: an ill-formed code cannot exist as a
`TariffCode`, so no handler downstream has to re-check it. The cost is that a
parse failure is now a framework-level 400 with a body you did not write, which
is exactly the problem ex6 fixes.

## ex4 - BindAsync for a type assembled from a request

`DeclarantContext` needs two headers and a route value; there is no single string
to parse. `BindAsync` gets the whole `HttpContext`, so it can read all three, and
its `ParameterInfo` argument means one implementation can behave differently for
different parameter names if you ever need that.

Returning `null` is the trap. It is not an error — the parameter binds to null
and your handler runs. If the value is required, either throw a
`BadHttpRequestException` from `BindAsync` (which becomes a 400) or check for
null in the handler and answer deliberately.

## ex5 - AsParameters, and the eight-parameter smell

`[AsParameters]` binds each *member* of a struct or class using the normal rules,
recursively. Eight query parameters become one `DeclarationQuery`, which is
reusable, testable in isolation, and — the real win — has one obvious place to
put its validation method.

## ex6 - three failures, three honest answers

Malformed JSON, wrong content type, and a well-formed body with a bad value are
distinct events. Wiring `AddProblemDetails` plus a small `IExceptionHandler` for
`BadHttpRequestException` turns the first from a blank 400 into a document that
says the body could not be read; the 415 is already correct and just needs a
body; the third was always yours.

## ex7 - ValidationProblemDetails, and 400 versus 422

The `errors` member is `Dictionary<string, string[]>` — several messages per
field, and the key is the client's name for the field, not your property name.
On 400 versus 422: 400 means the request was malformed, 422 means it was
well-formed and semantically wrong. ASP.NET Core's own machinery uses 400 for
both, most APIs follow it, and the argument for 422 gets stronger the more your
clients distinguish "I sent garbage" from "you rejected my business rule". Pick
one, document it, never mix them per-endpoint.

## ex8 - IExceptionHandler

`IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns `bool`: `true` means handled, `false`
means "not mine, try the next one". Handlers run in registration order, so
specific ones go first and the catch-all goes last. Writing the problem document
through `IProblemDetailsService` rather than by hand means your
`CustomizeProblemDetails` hook still applies.

## challenge - the whole surface on one endpoint

Custom-bound type, `[AsParameters]`, field validation with several messages, a
domain exception translated by the handler, and one consistent document shape
across all of it.

## review1 - the read side

Headers, `Accept`, and a 415 you have to produce yourself. Different inputs, same
discipline: every rejection names what was wrong.

## Further reading

- [Parameter binding in minimal API apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/parameter-binding)
- [Handle errors in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling)
- [Problem details service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/web-api/handle-errors#problem-details-service)
- [RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457)
- [IExceptionHandler](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#iexceptionhandler)
lessons.fullReading:
# Reading — binding, validation and the shape of a refusal

## Why binding exists at all

An HTTP request is bytes: a method, a path, some headers, maybe a body. A C#
method wants `int declarationId, TariffCode code, LineRequest body`. Something
has to cross that gap, and every web framework in every language has a version of
it. What differs is how much of the crossing is visible.

ASP.NET Core MVC made it very visible and very configurable: value providers,
model binders, binder providers, a model metadata system, and validation woven
through it. That machinery is genuinely powerful — it will bind a deeply nested
form post into an object graph and collect per-property validation errors as it
goes — and it is also why an MVC request has a measurable fixed cost and why
diagnosing "why is this property null" involves reading framework source.

Minimal APIs took the opposite position. There is no value-provider abstraction
and no model metadata system. There is a fixed rule order, resolved once per
endpoint at build time, and two extension points on *your* types: `TryParse` and
`BindAsync`. The result is fast — the generated delegate does the minimum — and
predictable, at the price of doing less for you. Notably, it does no validation
at all.

## The build-time delegate

When the endpoint is built, the framework inspects the handler's `MethodInfo` and
emits a `RequestDelegate`. In .NET 7 and later this is often produced by the
request-delegate generator at compile time; otherwise it is built with expression
trees and compiled at startup. Either way, the work of deciding "this parameter
comes from the route value `id`, parsed with `int.TryParse`" happens once.

Two things follow. Startup gets slightly more expensive and every request gets
cheaper — the usual trade, and the right one for a server. And binding errors
that *can* be detected statically are detected at startup: two body parameters,
an unbindable type, a `[FromRoute]` naming a segment that does not exist. The
errors that cannot be detected statically — a client sending `quantity=lots` —
are the ones you have to design a response for.

## What the framework does with a binding failure

When a simple-type parse fails, the generated delegate records the failure,
logs it at debug level, sets the status to 400 and returns. Your handler is never
invoked. The response has no body.

That last sentence is the whole reason `AddProblemDetails` exists. Historically
ASP.NET Core would send bare status codes for framework-generated errors, and
API consumers received a 400 with nothing in it. `AddProblemDetails` registers
`IProblemDetailsService` and a middleware that, for any 4xx or 5xx response that
has not written a body, generates a minimal RFC 9457 document from the status
code. It is a safety net, not a replacement for deliberate errors: the document
it generates has a generic `title` derived from the status and no field names,
because at that point in the pipeline nobody knows which field failed.

Getting field names into a framework-generated 400 is genuinely not possible
through that path. The practical answer is to bind the value as a `string?` and
parse it yourself whenever the field name matters to the client — which is the
same trade sector DA1 made with route constraints. Structural precision costs you
a message; a message costs you a manual parse.

## Validation, and the hole where it isn't

Minimal APIs do not run data annotations. `[Required]`, `[Range]` and
`[StringLength]` on a record bound from the body are inert. This surprises people
migrating from controllers, where `[ApiController]` triggers automatic model
validation and returns a `ValidationProblemDetails` for free.

The omission is deliberate: automatic validation means a reflective pass over
every bound model on every request, and minimal APIs are aimed at the cases where
that cost is not wanted. The intended replacements, roughly in order of how much
ceremony they add:

- a plain method on the request type returning an errors dictionary, called at
  the top of the handler — no dependencies, completely explicit;
- an endpoint filter that validates one type, added to a group — from DA1, and
  the sweet spot for most APIs;
- `MiniValidation` or FluentValidation resolved from DI inside such a filter, for
  when the rules get real.

.NET 10 adds first-class validation support for minimal APIs, driven by a source
generator over annotated types, which closes the gap without the reflective cost.
On .NET 8 the filter is the answer.

## The status code argument

400 versus 422 is the one API-design argument that will outlive us all. The
positions, briefly:

- **400 for everything.** It is what the framework does, what `ValidationProblem`
  produces, and what most clients' error handling already special-cases. Clients
  that need detail read `errors`.
- **400 for malformed, 422 for well-formed-but-invalid.** RFC 9110 defines 422 as
  "the request was well-formed but was unable to be followed due to semantic
  errors", which is exactly what a failed business rule is. It lets a client
  distinguish "my serialiser is broken" from "the server disagrees with my data"
  without parsing bodies.

What matters far more than the choice is consistency, and that the body is a
problem document either way. An API that returns 400 with `errors` from one
endpoint and 422 with a plain string from another has made its own clients write
two error paths.

## Performance notes

Binding cost is dominated by the body: `System.Text.Json` deserialisation is the
expensive part and it scales with payload size. Query and route binding are span
parses and are effectively free. `BindAsync` is as expensive as you make it —
which is worth remembering, because it is an inviting place to put a database
lookup, and a `BindAsync` that hits a database has made every request to that
endpoint do I/O before your handler can decide whether it needed to.

`ValidationProblemDetails` allocates a dictionary and arrays per failure. That is
fine on an error path and would not be fine on a hot success path, which is
another argument for validating in a filter and returning early.

The source-generated JSON path matters at scale: adding a `JsonSerializerContext`
and registering it in `ConfigureHttpJsonOptions` removes reflection from
serialisation and is a requirement for native AOT.

## When not to reach for these tools

**Do not write `BindAsync` for something a `TryParse` can do.** It is more code,
it hides the source of the value, and it takes the type out of OpenAPI's
understanding — a `BindAsync` type appears in the generated document as nothing
useful unless you add metadata by hand.

**Do not use `[AsParameters]` for two parameters.** It buys grouping and one
validation site; below about four members it costs more than it returns.

**Do not use `CustomizeProblemDetails` for per-endpoint messages.** It runs for
everything, has no clean access to which endpoint produced the response, and
becomes a switch statement over paths.

**Do not translate exceptions into 400s.** An exception handler that maps
`Exception` to a client error has converted your bugs into the client's fault and
thrown away the stack trace. Map the specific domain exceptions you have decided
are part of the contract, return `false` for everything else, and let the last
handler produce a 500.

## Further reading

- [Parameter binding in minimal API applications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/parameter-binding)
- [Handle errors in ASP.NET Core APIs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/web-api/handle-errors)
- [Problem details and `IProblemDetailsService`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#problem-details)
- [RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457)
- [System.Text.Json source generation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/serialization/system-text-json/source-generation)

## Exercise 1 — four sources, one signature

Edit `src/Api/V3DA02_BindingValidation/Ex1.cs`. The declaration store is given at
the bottom of the file: declarations `101` (office `LHR`, status `open`) and `102`
(office `DOV`, status `closed`).

Map `POST /v3da02/declarations/{declarationId:int}/echo` with a handler that
takes its four inputs from four different places, each named **explicitly** with
an attribute even where the default would agree:

- `declarationId` from the route
- `draft` from the query string, a `bool?` defaulting to `false` when absent
- `declarant` from the **header** `X-Declarant`, required
- `body` from the JSON body: `record EchoRequest(string Note)`

Answer 200 with:

```json
{"declarationId":101,"draft":true,"declarant":"asmith","note":"first pass"}
```

for `POST /v3da02/declarations/101/echo?draft=true` with `X-Declarant: asmith`
and body `{"note":"first pass"}`.

Then map `GET /v3da02/declarations/{declarationId:int}/mismatch` with a handler
whose parameter is called `id`, not `declarationId`, and which returns
`{"id":<value or null>}`. Requesting `/v3da02/declarations/101/mismatch` must
return `{"id":null}`, and `/v3da02/declarations/101/mismatch?id=7` must return
`{"id":7}`.

That second endpoint is the exercise. The route-name rule matches on the
parameter's **name**; when it does not match, the parameter falls through to the
query-string rule and binds to nothing, with no error anywhere. Bind `int? id`,
not `int`, or the framework will 400 the request before you can observe it.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da02_binding_validation_problems ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every parameter has exactly one source, chosen at build time. The attributes do
not change what the framework *can* do; they remove the guessing from what it
*will* do.

## Hint 2

The header attribute needs the wire name, because the wire name has a hyphen and
a C# parameter cannot:

    [FromHeader(Name = "X-Correlation-Id")] string correlationId

## Hint 3

`bool? draft` plus `draft ?? false` in the projection gives you the default
without making the parameter required. The decision left to you: `draft` as
`bool?` with a coalesce, or `bool draft = false` with a default value — both
work, and one of them changes what happens when the client sends `?draft=maybe`.

## Hint 4

For the mismatch endpoint, resist fixing the name. The whole point is to see the
silent fallthrough with your own eyes.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Predict the mismatch endpoint's answer before running it. Most people say "400,
surely" or "it binds anyway, the route value is right there". It is neither: it
is a successful 200 with a null, which is why this bug survives code review.

## Hint 2

If `X-Declarant` comes back empty, check the attribute. `[FromHeader] string
declarant` looks for a header literally called `declarant`; the `Name` property
is not optional here.

## Hint 3

Watch for two body parameters. If you accidentally leave a parameter the binder
cannot place — a misspelt service type, say — it falls through to rule 7 and the
application refuses to start with a message about multiple body parameters. That
message is almost never about the body; it is about the parameter you forgot to
give a source.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the query string is a multimap, not a dictionary

Edit `src/Api/V3DA02_BindingValidation/Ex2.cs`. Map
`GET /v3da02/lines/filter` with three parameters over the **same** key, `code`,
plus one over `office`:

```csharp
private static IResult Filter(
    [FromQuery(Name = "code")] string[] codesArray,
    [FromQuery(Name = "code")] StringValues codesValues,
    [FromQuery(Name = "office")] string? office)
```

Return 200 with:

```json
{"arrayCount":n,"valuesCount":m,"first":"...","officeIsNull":true,
 "officeIsEmpty":false}
```

where `first` is the first array element or `null` when there are none.

The gate walks four query strings and asserts the exact answers:

| query | arrayCount | valuesCount | first |
|---|---|---|---|
| *(none)* | 0 | 0 | `null` |
| `?code=8471.30` | 1 | 1 | `"8471.30"` |
| `?code=8471.30&code=6109.10` | 2 | 2 | `"8471.30"` |
| `?code=` | 1 | 1 | `""` |

The last row is the one worth staring at. A key that is present with an empty
value is **not** the same as an absent key, and a filter written as
`codes.Contains(line.Code)` over that array matches nothing at all — a
"filter that returns no rows" bug that looks like missing data.

Then map `GET /v3da02/lines/matching?code=a&code=b`, which returns the lines
whose `Code` is in the list, ordered by `Id`, and treats an **absent or empty**
`code` as "no filter, return everything". `?code=` must return all three lines,
not zero.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da02_binding_validation_problems ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`?a=1&a=2` is legal HTTP and has no dictionary equivalent. Everything odd about
query binding follows from the framework modelling it honestly as a multimap.

## Hint 2

`StringValues` is the raw shape and answers questions the array cannot:

    var supplied = codesValues.Count > 0;
    var meaningful = codesValues.Where(v => !string.IsNullOrEmpty(v)).ToArray();

`StringValues.IsNullOrEmpty(values)` is true for both "absent" and "one empty
string", which is usually the test you actually want.

## Hint 3

For `matching`, filter the array down to non-empty entries first, then treat a
zero-length result as "no filter". The decision left to you: is `?code=&code=x` a
one-code filter or a malformed request? Pick, and be able to defend it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the four expected rows on paper before you run anything. Almost everyone
gets row 4 wrong, and getting it wrong here is much cheaper than getting it wrong
in a report that silently returns nothing.

## Hint 2

If `arrayCount` and `valuesCount` ever disagree, you have bound them to different
keys. Both attributes must say `Name = "code"`; without the `Name`, the binder
uses the parameter names `codesArray` and `codesValues`, and both come back
empty.

## Hint 3

`office` needs two booleans because null and empty are different states and JSON
flattens them if you are careless. `office is null` for absent, `office is ""`
for `?office=`. If your `officeIsNull` is true for `?office=`, something coalesced
on the way through.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — a type the binder understands

Edit `src/Api/V3DA02_BindingValidation/Ex3.cs`. Implement
`readonly record struct TariffCode(string Value) : IParsable<TariffCode>` so a
tariff code binds directly from a route segment or a query value.

A valid code is exactly seven characters: four ASCII digits, a `.`, two ASCII
digits — `8471.30` is valid, `847.130`, `8471.3`, `84A1.30` and `8471.30 ` are
not. `TryParse` returns `false` for every invalid input and **never throws**;
`Parse` throws `FormatException` with the message
`Tariff codes are four digits, a dot, two digits.`. `ToString()` returns the
value.

Then map:

- `GET /v3da02/tariffs/{code}` — parameter typed `TariffCode`, returning
  `{"code":"8471.30","known":true}` where `known` is whether any line in the
  store carries that code. `GET /v3da02/tariffs/nope` is a framework **400** with
  an empty body, and you are not to fix that here — observe it.
- `GET /v3da02/tariffs/lenient?code=x` — parameter typed `string?`, parsed with
  `TariffCode.TryParse` by hand, answering **400** with a validation problem
  keyed `"code"` and message `Tariff codes are four digits, a dot, two digits.`
  when it fails.

The pair is the argument. Binding the strong type means an invalid code cannot
exist downstream, and buys you a 400 with no explanation. Binding a string and
parsing yourself costs three lines and buys you a message with the field name in
it. Neither is wrong; know which one you chose.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da02_binding_validation_problems ex3
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it from the failure the gate cannot see. `TryParse` throwing is the
classic error: an `IndexOutOfRangeException` from `s[4]` on a three-character
input becomes a **500** from inside model binding, which is the least debuggable
error in this entire sector.

## Hint 2

Test the type before you wire the endpoint. Six lines in a scratch console over
`8471.30`, `847.130`, `8471.3`, `84A1.30`, `""`, `null` and a trailing-space
string will find every bounds bug in under a minute, and you cannot get that
signal through an HTTP gate.

## Hint 3

For `lenient`, note that you are re-implementing nothing: call
`TariffCode.TryParse(code, null, out var parsed)`. The validation rule lives in
exactly one place, and the endpoint chooses only the *reporting*. If you find
yourself re-checking the format inside the endpoint, back out — duplicated
validation is how two versions of a rule get shipped.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — BindAsync, for a value that is not one string

Edit `src/Api/V3DA02_BindingValidation/Ex4.cs`. Implement

```csharp
public record DeclarantContext(string Declarant, string Office, int DeclarationId)
{
    public static ValueTask<DeclarantContext?> BindAsync(HttpContext http, ParameterInfo parameter)
}
```

It assembles itself from **three** places in the request: the `X-Declarant`
header, the `X-Office` header, and the `declarationId` route value. No single
string exists to parse, so `TryParse` cannot express this.

Rules:

- either header missing or whitespace → return `null`
- `X-Office` present but not three uppercase ASCII letters → throw
  `new BadHttpRequestException("X-Office must be three capitals.", 400)`
- otherwise return the assembled record

Map `GET /v3da02/declarations/{declarationId:int}/context` with a
`DeclarantContext? context` parameter:

- `context is null` → **401** problem, `title` = `Declarant headers required`
- otherwise 200 `{"declarant":"asmith","office":"LHR","declarationId":101}`

And map `GET /v3da02/declarations/{declarationId:int}/strict-context` with a
**non-nullable** `DeclarantContext context` parameter, returning the same body on
success. Send it no headers and you get a framework **400**, because a
non-nullable parameter whose `BindAsync` returned null is a binding failure.

Three outcomes from one method, and they are worth naming: returning null is
*not* an error, throwing `BadHttpRequestException` *is* one, and the parameter's
nullability decides what null means.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da02_binding_validation_problems ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`BindAsync` is the escape hatch for values that are a function of the request
rather than of one token in it. The signature is fixed: `public static
ValueTask<T?> BindAsync(HttpContext, ParameterInfo)`.

## Hint 2

Reading the route value inside `BindAsync`, on a different type:

    var raw = http.Request.RouteValues["shipmentId"] as string;
    if (!int.TryParse(raw, out var shipmentId))
        throw new BadHttpRequestException("Bad shipment id.", 400);

`RouteValues` is populated by the time binding runs, so the route is available
even though you are outside the handler.

## Hint 3

Guard the headers, validate the office, then
`ValueTask.FromResult<DeclarantContext?>(new(...))`. The decision left to you:
should a missing header be null or a throw? The prompt fixes it as null so you
can see both behaviours from one implementation — say which you would ship.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two endpoints, one binder, different failure modes. Before writing anything,
state what you expect `/strict-context` with no headers to do. The answer follows
entirely from "null is not an error, but a null for a non-nullable parameter is".

## Hint 2

If both endpoints return 401, your strict parameter is still nullable. If both
return 400, you nullable-annotated nothing and the compiler is not helping —
`DeclarantContext?` versus `DeclarantContext` is the whole difference and it is
one character.

## Hint 3

`BadHttpRequestException` is special-cased by the framework: its `StatusCode` is
used for the response. Throwing anything else from `BindAsync` gives you a 500,
which is a fair description of a bug in your binder and a terrible description of
a bad header. That distinction — client error versus server error, chosen by
exception type — is worth carrying into ex8.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — eight query parameters, one type, one validation site

Edit `src/Api/V3DA02_BindingValidation/Ex5.cs`. Define

```csharp
public readonly struct DeclarationQuery
{
    [FromQuery] public string? Office { get; init; }
    [FromQuery] public string? Status { get; init; }
    [FromQuery(Name = "code")] public string[] Codes { get; init; }
    [FromQuery] public int? MinQuantity { get; init; }
    [FromQuery] public int? Page { get; init; }
    [FromQuery] public int? Size { get; init; }
    [FromQuery] public string? Sort { get; init; }

    public Dictionary<string, string[]> Validate()
}
```

and map `GET /v3da02/search` taking `[AsParameters] DeclarationQuery query`.

`Validate` returns an empty dictionary when the query is acceptable, and
otherwise one entry per offending field, using the **client's** names:

- `page` — `Must be 1 or more.` when below 1
- `size` — `Between 1 and 100.` when below 1 or above 100
- `minQuantity` — `Must not be negative.` when below 0
- `status` — `Must be open or closed.` when present and neither
- `sort` — `Must be id, office or status.` when present and none of those
- `office` — `Must be three capitals.` when present and not three uppercase
  letters

A non-empty dictionary is a **400** `ValidationProblem`. Otherwise apply the
filters (all conjunctive; absent means no filter; `code` uses the ex2 rule that
empty entries do not filter), sort ascending by the requested field defaulting to
`id`, paginate with `page` defaulting to 1 and `size` to 20, and return:

```json
{"page":1,"size":20,"total":2,"items":[{"id":101,"office":"LHR","status":"open"}]}
```

`total` is the count **before** pagination — the number clients need to render a
pager, and the one most often reported wrong.

The gate sends `?page=0&size=500&status=maybe` and expects exactly three keys in
`errors`, so accumulate every failure rather than returning on the first one.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da02_binding_validation_problems ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`[AsParameters]` binds each member of the type using the ordinary rules — the
struct is not deserialised from anything, it is assembled parameter by parameter.
Which means the attributes on the properties are the same attributes you would
have written on the handler.

## Hint 2

Accumulating rather than short-circuiting:

    var errors = new Dictionary<string, string[]>();
    if (Page is < 1) errors["page"] = ["Must be 1 or more."];
    if (Size is < 1 or > 100) errors["size"] = ["Between 1 and 100."];
    return errors;

`Page is < 1` on an `int?` is false when it is null, which is the behaviour you
want for optional filters and is easy to lose by writing `Page.Value < 1`.

## Hint 3

Compose the query as `IEnumerable<Declaration>`, applying each filter only when
its input is present, then take `total` from the filtered sequence before
`Skip`/`Take`. The decision left to you: is an unknown `sort` value a 400 or a
silent fallback to `id`? The prompt says 400 — be able to argue the other side.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Count the assertions. The gate's bad request has three problems and expects three
keys. A validator written as a chain of early returns produces one, passes a
casual read, and fails here — which is the same reason a real client has to fix
its request three times instead of once.

## Hint 2

If `total` equals the number of items you returned, you computed it after
paginating. Materialise the filtered sequence once (`.ToList()`), take `Count`
from that, then page it — otherwise you also enumerate the source twice for no
reason.

## Hint 3

The struct must be `readonly` with `init` accessors and *not* have a
parameterless-constructor requirement you have broken. If binding silently gives
you all-null members, check that the properties are public and settable through
`init`; `[AsParameters]` matches names case-insensitively and will simply skip
anything it cannot write.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — three different failures, three honest bodies

Edit `src/Api/V3DA02_BindingValidation/Ex6.cs`. `Ex6Services` registers
`AddProblemDetails` with a `CustomizeProblemDetails` hook that, for **every**
document the framework generates, sets:

- `Instance` to the request path, if not already set
- an extension `traceId` = `Activity.Current?.Id ?? HttpContext.TraceIdentifier`
- an extension `service` = `"v3da02"`

Then map `POST /v3da02/strict/lines` taking `record LineRequest(string Code, int
Quantity)` and returning 201 `{"code":"...","quantity":n}` on success.

The gate sends four requests and asserts four distinct answers:

1. body `{"code":"8471.30","quantity":4}`, `Content-Type: application/json` →
   **201**
2. body `{"code":"8471.30",}` (trailing comma), `Content-Type: application/json`
   → **400**, `application/problem+json`, `title` = `Malformed request body`,
   and a `traceId` extension
3. body `code=8471.30`, `Content-Type: text/plain` → **415**,
   `application/problem+json`, with a `traceId` extension
4. body `{"code":"99","quantity":-4}` → **400**, `application/problem+json`,
   `errors` containing **both** `code` and `quantity`

Row 2 needs an `IExceptionHandler` for `BadHttpRequestException` — malformed JSON
surfaces as one, wrapping a `JsonException` — registered in `Ex6Services` with
`AddExceptionHandler`. Row 3 needs nothing but `AddProblemDetails`: the 415 is
already correct, it simply had no body before. Row 4 is ordinary handler
validation: `code` must parse as a `TariffCode`, `quantity` must be positive.

Say the three layers out loud when you are done. One is the framework refusing to
read the request, one is the framework refusing the media type, one is you
refusing the content. Only the third one could ever have been written in your
handler.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da02_binding_validation_problems ex6
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Reproduce row 2 by hand with curl before writing the handler, and read what you
currently get. A blank 400 is the default, and seeing it is what makes the rest
of the exercise feel necessary rather than ceremonial.

## Hint 2

If row 3 comes back with an empty body, `AddProblemDetails` is registered but the
response was already committed, or the middleware is not in the pipeline. If rows
2 and 3 have no `traceId`, you wrote the document yourself with
`Results.Problem(...)` instead of going through `IProblemDetailsService` — the
hook only runs for documents the service generates.

## Hint 3

Row 4 wants both keys in one response. Build the dictionary, add both entries,
then return once. And note the asymmetry worth defending: `quantity: -4` is a
number the binder accepted and you rejected, while `quantity: "four"` never
reaches you at all. Two different 400s, one of which you cannot make specific
without binding the field as a string.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — the errors dictionary, and the 422 argument

Edit `src/Api/V3DA02_BindingValidation/Ex7.cs`. Map
`POST /v3da02/declarations/{declarationId:int}/submit` taking

```csharp
record SubmitRequest(string Office, List<LineRequest> Lines, string? Reference)
```

and validate it into a single `Dictionary<string, string[]>` where the keys are
the **client's JSON paths**, not your property names:

- `office` — `Must be three capitals.` and, additionally, `Must be a known
  office.` when it is not `LHR` or `DOV`. A value of `xx` therefore produces
  **two** messages under one key.
- `lines` — `At least one line is required.` when the list is null or empty
- `lines[0].code`, `lines[1].code`, … — `Tariff codes are four digits, a dot,
  two digits.` for each offending line, indexed by its position
- `lines[i].quantity` — `Must be positive.`
- `reference` — `Must be at most 16 characters.` when present and longer

Return **422** with an `HttpValidationProblemDetails` whose `title` is
`The declaration was rejected.` and whose `status` is 422, plus an extension
`declarationId`. On success return 200 `{"declarationId":n,"lines":m}`.

Two rules are separate from validation and come **first**, in this order: an
unknown declaration is a **404**, and a declaration whose status is `closed` is a
**409** problem titled `Declaration closed`. Declaration `102` is closed, so the
gate uses it to check that a closed declaration with a perfectly valid body still
gets the 409 — existence and state before content.

422 rather than 400 is the deliberate choice here: the request was well-formed
JSON that the server understood and refused on business grounds. Be able to argue
for 400 too; what you must not do is pick per endpoint.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da02_binding_validation_problems ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The `errors` member is a dictionary of arrays, not a dictionary of strings.
Two problems with one field is the case that shape exists for, and most
validators quietly overwrite instead.

## Hint 2

Indexed keys are built, not declared:

    for (var i = 0; i < items.Count; i++)
    {
        if (items[i].Weight <= 0)
            errors[$"items[{i}].weight"] = ["Must be positive."];
    }

The bracket-and-dot spelling is the JSON-path convention most clients already
understand, and it lets a form highlight the exact row.

## Hint 3

`TypedResults.ValidationProblem` takes `statusCode`, `title` and `extensions`
overloads, so you do not have to construct the details object by hand. The
decision left to you: when a field has two failures, do you emit both messages or
stop at the first? The prompt says both — decide what you would do when one of
the checks is expensive.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Order the three refusals before you write them: 404, then 409, then 422. Test it
by sending a *valid* body to declaration `102`. Any implementation that validates
first will produce a 422 there and be wrong in a way that no valid-input test
would ever catch.

## Hint 2

If `office: "xx"` yields one message, you assigned twice to the same key —
`errors["office"] = [a]; errors["office"] = [b];` keeps only the second. Collect
into a `List<string>` per key and assign once at the end.

## Hint 3

Check the status in the body, not just on the response. `ValidationProblem` sets

between the two — 422 on the wire, 400 in the JSON — is a real bug that clients
trip over, because many of them read the body's `status` in preference to the

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — an exception handler chain that knows when to say no

Edit `src/Api/V3DA02_BindingValidation/Ex8.cs`. The domain code is given and
throws two exceptions:

```csharp
public class DeclarationClosedException(int declarationId) : Exception("Closed.")
{
    public int DeclarationId { get; } = declarationId;
}

public class TariffUnknownException(string code) : Exception("Unknown tariff.")
{
    public string Code { get; } = code;
}
```

`Ex8Services` registers **three** exception handlers, in this order:

1. `ClosedHandler` — `DeclarationClosedException` → **409**, `title` =
   `Declaration closed`, extension `declarationId`
2. `TariffHandler` — `TariffUnknownException` → **422**, `title` =
   `Unknown tariff code`, extension `code`
3. `LastResortHandler` — anything at all → **500**, `title` = `Unexpected
   failure`, extension `handled` = `"last-resort"`, and it must **log** the
   exception before writing

Every handler writes through `IProblemDetailsService`, and every one returns
`false` for exceptions it does not own.

Map `POST /v3da02/audit/{declarationId:int}/lines` taking a `LineRequest`. The
handler calls `V3DA02Audit.Add(declarationId, body)` — given, and not to be
wrapped in `try`/`catch` — which throws `DeclarationClosedException` for
declaration `102`, `TariffUnknownException` for any code not in the store, and
`InvalidOperationException("boom")` when the code is exactly `0000.00`.
Otherwise it returns a `Line` and the endpoint answers **201**.

Expected: `102` → 409, an unknown-but-well-formed code → 422, `0000.00` → 500
with `handled: "last-resort"`, a good request → 201.

The ordering is the lesson. `LastResortHandler` returns `true` for everything, so
registering it first would swallow the other two and every domain error in the
application would become a 500 — a failure mode that produces no compiler
warning, no startup error, and a very confusing afternoon.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da02_binding_validation_problems ex8
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Prove the ordering by breaking it. Register `LastResortHandler` first, run the
gate, and watch the 409 and the 422 both become 500s. Then put it back. The point
is that nothing anywhere told you it was wrong.

## Hint 2

If everything returns 500 even in the right order, your first two handlers are
returning `true` for exceptions they did not handle, or they are not returning
`false` at all — a handler that falls off the end of the method returning `true`
by accident stops the chain silently.

## Hint 3

Logging belongs in `LastResortHandler` and nowhere else here. A 409 for a closed
declaration is not an incident and does not deserve an error log entry; a 500 is,
and losing its stack trace to a tidy problem document is exactly how an outage
becomes unexplainable. Take `ILogger<LastResortHandler>` and log at `Error` with
the exception as the first argument.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — one endpoint, every layer

Honest difficulty note: no individual piece here is new. The difficulty is
ordering six refusals correctly and keeping one document shape across all of
them.

Edit `src/Api/V3DA02_BindingValidation/Challenge.cs`. Map

```
PUT /v3da02/declarations/{declarationId:int}/lines/{code}
```

with this signature — and no other parameters:

```csharp
private static IResult Replace(
    int declarationId,
    TariffCode code,
    DeclarantContext? declarant,
    [AsParameters] ReplaceOptions options,
```
