that a rule written inside a handler cannot be found, cannot be tested without
the handler, cannot be reused by the endpoint next door, and cannot be applied to
a group so that a new endpoint inherits it by default. The rules end up scattered
in proportion to how many places need them, and then one of the places is missed.

ASP.NET Core's answer is a small algebra with three parts, and once you can state
it, most of the API stops needing to be memorised.

## Concept — policy, requirement, handler

**A policy is an AND of requirements.** `AddPolicy("x", p => p
.RequireAuthenticatedUser().RequireClaim("panel"))` builds a policy with two
requirements, and both must be satisfied. There is no `Or` on the builder,
deliberately.

**A requirement is an OR of handlers.** A requirement is a marker object — often
literally empty — implementing `IAuthorizationRequirement`. Handlers are
registered against a requirement type, and *any* handler calling
`context.Succeed(requirement)` satisfies it. This is where "or" lives: two
handlers, two independent reasons to say yes.

**A failure beats every success.** `context.Fail()` is a veto. It does not matter
that another handler already succeeded on that requirement, or that every other
requirement passed — a single `Fail` makes the whole evaluation fail, and by
default the remaining handlers are not even run. This asymmetry is what lets you
write "…unless the proposal is sealed" as a separate handler rather than as a
clause inside every other one.

Two more facts that turn those three sentences into working code.

**A handler can be typed on a resource.** `AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement>`
sees the requirement and the principal. `AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement,
TResource>` additionally receives a resource object, and — this is the part that
matters — it *only runs* when a resource of that type was supplied. Which brings
us to the second fact:

**`RequireAuthorization` supplies the `HttpContext` as the resource.** When the
authorization middleware evaluates a policy, `context.Resource` is the
`HttpContext`. That is genuinely useful — it is how a handler reads a route value
— and it means a handler typed on your own domain object never fires under
`RequireAuthorization`. To decide about a loaded entity you must call
`IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, policyName)` yourself, from
inside the handler, after loading it.

That last point is not a limitation to work around; it is a consequence of
ordering. "May this reviewer see proposal 41" cannot be answered before proposal
41 has been fetched, and the middleware runs long before any fetching happens.

## Concept — where policies attach

An endpoint, a group, or the whole application:

```csharp
app.MapGet("/v3da04/panels", ListPanels).RequireAuthorization("PanelMember");

var board = app.MapGroup("/v3da04/board").RequireAuthorization("BoardStaff");

options.FallbackPolicy = new AuthorizationPolicyBuilder()
    .RequireAuthenticatedUser().Build();
```

The fallback policy is the interesting one. It applies to every endpoint that has
**no** authorization metadata at all, which turns "forgot to protect it" from the
default into an explicit `AllowAnonymous`. The default policy, by contrast,
applies when you write `RequireAuthorization()` with no arguments.

`AllowAnonymous` beats everything — group policies, fallback policies, an
`[Authorize]` on the same endpoint. It is metadata that the authorization
middleware looks for first and honours unconditionally, which is exactly the
opt-out mechanism sector DA1 described in the abstract.

## Concept — where a rule can be answered from

Before writing any policy, ask what the rule needs to know, because that decides
where it can live.

A rule that needs only the **token** — "must be an authenticated employee", "must
hold the `proposal.decide` permission" — can be answered by the middleware,
before the handler runs, and should be, because refusing early costs nothing and
keeps the rule visible at the endpoint.

A rule that needs the **request** — "the panel in the URL must match the caller's
panel" — can also be answered by the middleware, through the `HttpContext`
resource, at the cost of stringly-typed route lookups.

A rule that needs a **stored object** — "must be assigned to this proposal",
"unless a conflict is declared" — cannot be answered until the object is loaded,
which is inside the handler. No amount of attribute cleverness moves that
boundary; frameworks that appear to have moved it have only hidden the load.

Most real endpoints have rules from at least two of those categories, and the
resulting shape is the same every time: a declarative policy at the endpoint for
the token-level rules, and an explicit `AuthorizeAsync` call after loading for
the rest. Getting comfortable with that split — rather than trying to force
everything into one mechanism — is most of what this sector is for.

## What this sector drills

The domain is a **research grant review board** under `/v3da04/...`: proposals,
reviewers, panels, and conflicts of interest. The conflict of interest is the
useful part — it is a rule that is genuinely about a *pair* of things, a reviewer
and a proposal, and therefore cannot be expressed as a claim check.

Exercise 1 builds a policy from stock requirements and re-establishes 401 versus
403 in this new setting. Exercise 2 uses `RequireAssertion` with the `HttpContext`
resource to read a route value. Exercises 3 and 4 write a requirement and its
handlers, first one and then two, so the OR becomes concrete. Exercise 5 is the
resource-based check: load the proposal, then ask.

Exercise 6 is the veto: a sealed proposal that nobody may touch, written as a
handler that only ever fails. Exercise 7 is fallback and default policies plus
`AllowAnonymous`. Exercise 8 writes an `IAuthorizationPolicyProvider` so
`RequireAuthorization("permission:proposal.read")` works without registering
every permission by hand.

The challenge combines a dynamic policy, a resource handler and a veto on one
endpoint. The review replaces the 403 body with a problem document by
implementing `IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler`.

One framing to carry through: authorization code should read like the policy
document it implements. If your organisation's rule is "a panel member may read
any proposal on their panel, unless they have declared a conflict", there should
be a handler called something like `PanelMembershipHandler` and another called
`ConflictOfInterestHandler`, and the second should fail. When the rule changes,
you should know which file to open.

# Reading - dotnet/v3da04_authorization_policies

## Notes

**The evaluation loop, exactly.** `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync` builds
an `AuthorizationHandlerContext` holding the policy's requirements, the
principal, and the resource. It resolves every registered `IAuthorizationHandler`
from DI and calls each one with that context. Each handler looks through
`context.PendingRequirements` for requirements it understands and calls
`Succeed` or `Fail`. Afterwards, the result is `Succeeded` only if nothing failed
and every requirement was succeeded at least once.

**`context.Succeed(requirement)` takes the requirement instance.** Not the type —
the instance from the context. This matters when the same requirement type is
registered twice with different parameters: succeeding requirement A must not
satisfy requirement B.

**`Fail()` short-circuits by default.** `AuthorizationOptions
.InvokeHandlersAfterFailure` is `true` by default, which means remaining handlers
*do* still run; what `Fail` guarantees is that the final result is a failure
regardless of any success. Set it to `false` and evaluation stops at the first
failure, which is faster and loses the ability to collect every reason.

**`AuthorizationHandler<TReq, TResource>` filters on resource type.** The base
class checks `context.Resource is TResource` and returns without calling your
override when it is not. This is why a handler typed on `Proposal` is silently
inert under `RequireAuthorization` — the resource there is the `HttpContext`, and
nothing anywhere reports the mismatch.

**Resource-based checks are explicit calls.** Inject `IAuthorizationService`,
load the entity, then `await authorization.AuthorizeAsync(user, entity,
policyName)`. The result has `Succeeded` and, when it fails,
`Failure.FailedRequirements` — which is how you produce a 403 that says which
rule refused.

**404 before 403, usually.** Deciding about a resource requires the resource, so
an unknown id must be a 404. Whether an *existing* resource the caller may not
see should be 404 or 403 is a genuine policy question — 403 confirms existence,
404 hides it — and the answer depends on whether the id space is guessable and
whether existence is itself sensitive.

**`AllowAnonymous` wins.** The middleware checks for
`IAllowAnonymous` in the endpoint metadata before evaluating anything and skips
authorization entirely when it finds it. Group policies, fallback policies and
`[Authorize]` on the same endpoint all lose to it.

**Policy names are strings resolved through `IAuthorizationPolicyProvider`.** The
default provider looks up a dictionary populated by `AddPolicy`. Replacing it
lets you parse the name — `"permission:proposal.read"` — and build a policy on
demand, which is how permission systems with hundreds of names stay manageable.

## ex1 - stock requirements, and the same two refusals

`RequireAuthenticatedUser`, `RequireClaim`, `RequireRole` and `RequireAssertion`
are shorthands that append built-in requirement types. The 401-versus-403 rule
from DA3 is unchanged: no identity from the endpoint's schemes means challenge,
an identity that fails a policy means forbid.

## ex2 - the assertion, and the resource that is an HttpContext

`RequireAssertion(context => ...)` receives the `AuthorizationHandlerContext`,
whose `Resource` under the middleware is the `HttpContext`. Casting it and
reading `RouteValues` is legitimate and is the intended use — it is how "the
panel in the URL must match the caller's panel claim" is expressed without a
custom requirement.

The cost is that the rule is now a lambda in `Program.cs`-adjacent code: not
named, not unit-testable in isolation, not reusable. Assertions are for rules
that are genuinely one line and genuinely local.

## ex3 - a requirement and its handler

The requirement carries the *parameters* of the rule — a minimum seniority, a
required panel — and the handler carries the *logic*. Splitting them that way is
what lets one handler serve many configured instances of the same rule.

## ex4 - two handlers, one requirement

The second handler is the OR. Writing it as a second registration rather than as
an extra clause in the first buys you three things: each reason is separately
named, each is separately testable, and adding a third reason later touches no
existing file.

## ex5 - the decision needs the thing

Load, then ask. The endpoint gains an `IAuthorizationService` parameter and three
lines. The ordering — 404, then authorize, then validate — matters: validating
first tells a caller with no rights at all which of their fields were malformed,
which is a small information leak and a large annoyance.

## ex6 - the veto

A sealed proposal is refused for everybody, including the chair whose handler
already succeeded. That is only expressible because `Fail` outranks `Succeed`. In
a system where refusal were merely "not succeeding", the seal would have to be
checked inside every other handler, and the day someone adds a handler and
forgets is the day the seal stops working.

## ex7 - fallback, default, and the anonymous escape

The fallback policy makes "unprotected" a thing you have to write down. It
applies only to endpoints with no authorization metadata, so an endpoint with any
`RequireAuthorization` is unaffected, and `AllowAnonymous` opts out cleanly.

## ex8 - policies generated from their names

`IAuthorizationPolicyProvider` has three members; the interesting one is
`GetPolicyAsync(string name)`. Parse a convention out of the name, build a policy,
cache it. Always delegate unknown names to the default provider rather than
returning null for them, or every stock policy in the application disappears.

## challenge - all three at once

A dynamic permission policy, a resource handler that needs the loaded proposal,
and a veto that beats it.

## review1 - the body of a 403

`IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler` sits between the middleware and the
response and can turn `Forbidden` into a problem document naming the failed
requirement. Useful, and easy to overshare with — the same disclosure judgement
as DA3's `error_description`.

## Further reading

- [Policy-based authorization in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/policies)
- [Resource-based authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/resourcebased)
- [Custom authorization policy providers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/iauthorizationpolicyprovider)
- [Simple authorization and the fallback policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/simple)
- [Authorization middleware result handlers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/authorizationmiddlewareresulthandler)

# V3·DA4 — Authorization policies, requirements and resource checks

## 1. The algebra

```
policy      = requirement AND requirement AND …
requirement = handler OR handler OR …
any Fail()  ⇒ the whole evaluation fails
```

```csharp
services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy("PanelMember", policy => policy
        .AddAuthenticationSchemes(V3DA04Jwt.Scheme)
        .RequireAuthenticatedUser()
        .RequireClaim("panel"));
```

Two requirements, both mandatory. There is no `.Or(...)`; an OR is two handlers
against one requirement.

## 2. A requirement and its handlers

```csharp
public class SeniorityRequirement(int minimum) : IAuthorizationRequirement
{
    public int Minimum { get; } = minimum;      // the rule's parameters
}

public class SeniorityHandler : AuthorizationHandler<SeniorityRequirement>
{
    protected override Task HandleRequirementAsync(
        AuthorizationHandlerContext context, SeniorityRequirement requirement)
    {
        var grade = int.TryParse(context.User.FindFirst("grade")?.Value, out var g) ? g : 0;
        if (grade >= requirement.Minimum) context.Succeed(requirement);
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

public class ChairHandler : AuthorizationHandler<SeniorityRequirement>
{
    protected override Task HandleRequirementAsync(
        AuthorizationHandlerContext context, SeniorityRequirement requirement)
    {
        if (context.User.IsInRole("chair")) context.Succeed(requirement);
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
```

Both registered as `services.AddSingleton<IAuthorizationHandler, …>()`. Either
one succeeding is enough. Note that neither calls `Fail` — a handler that cannot
say yes should say nothing, because failing would veto its sibling.

## 3. Resource-based checks

```csharp
public class ReviewerAssignmentHandler
    : AuthorizationHandler<ProposalAccessRequirement, Proposal>
{
    protected override Task HandleRequirementAsync(
        AuthorizationHandlerContext context,
        ProposalAccessRequirement requirement,
        Proposal resource)
    {
        if (resource.Reviewers.Contains(context.User.Identity?.Name ?? ""))
            context.Succeed(requirement);
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
```

Invoked from the endpoint, after loading:

```csharp
var proposal = board.Find(id);
if (proposal is null) return TypedResults.NotFound();

var decision = await authorization.AuthorizeAsync(user, proposal, "ReadProposal");
if (!decision.Succeeded)
    return TypedResults.Forbid(authenticationSchemes: [V3DA04Jwt.Scheme]);
```

Under `RequireAuthorization("ReadProposal")` this handler would never run: the
middleware passes the `HttpContext` as the resource, and the base class filters
on type.

## 4. The veto

```csharp
public class SealHandler : AuthorizationHandler<ProposalAccessRequirement, Proposal>
{
    protected override Task HandleRequirementAsync(
        AuthorizationHandlerContext context,
        ProposalAccessRequirement requirement,
        Proposal resource)
    {
        if (resource.Sealed) context.Fail(
            new AuthorizationFailureReason(this, "The proposal is sealed."));
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}
```

`Fail` with a reason is better than bare `Fail`: the reason reaches
`AuthorizationResult.Failure.FailureReasons`, which is what a good 403 body is
built from.

## 5. Reading the request from a policy

```csharp
.AddPolicy("OwnPanel", policy => policy
    .RequireAuthenticatedUser()
    .RequireAssertion(context =>
    {
        if (context.Resource is not HttpContext http) return false;
        var panel = http.Request.RouteValues["panel"]?.ToString();
        return panel is not null && context.User.HasClaim("panel", panel);
    }));
```

`context.Resource` is the `HttpContext` under the middleware — that is the
documented behaviour, not a hack.

## 6. Fallback, default, anonymous

```csharp
services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .SetFallbackPolicy(new AuthorizationPolicyBuilder()
        .AddAuthenticationSchemes(V3DA04Jwt.Scheme)
        .RequireAuthenticatedUser()
        .Build())
    .SetDefaultPolicy(…);

app.MapGet("/v3da04/health", () => "ok").AllowAnonymous();
```

| mechanism | applies to |
|---|---|
| fallback policy | endpoints with **no** authorization metadata |
| default policy | `RequireAuthorization()` with no arguments |
| `AllowAnonymous` | wins over all of the above |

## 7. Policies from their names

```csharp
public class PermissionPolicyProvider(IOptions<AuthorizationOptions> options)
    : IAuthorizationPolicyProvider
{
    private readonly DefaultAuthorizationPolicyProvider _fallback = new(options);

    public Task<AuthorizationPolicy> GetDefaultPolicyAsync() =>
        _fallback.GetDefaultPolicyAsync();

    public Task<AuthorizationPolicy?> GetFallbackPolicyAsync() =>
        _fallback.GetFallbackPolicyAsync();

    public Task<AuthorizationPolicy?> GetPolicyAsync(string policyName)
    {
        if (!policyName.StartsWith("permission:", StringComparison.Ordinal))
            return _fallback.GetPolicyAsync(policyName);   // never return null here

        var permission = policyName["permission:".Length..];
        return Task.FromResult<AuthorizationPolicy?>(new AuthorizationPolicyBuilder()
            .AddAuthenticationSchemes(V3DA04Jwt.Scheme)
            .RequireAuthenticatedUser()
            .RequireClaim("perm", permission)
            .Build());
    }
}
```

Register with `services.AddSingleton<IAuthorizationPolicyProvider,
PermissionPolicyProvider>()`. `GetPolicyAsync` is called **once per endpoint per
policy name** and the result is cached by the middleware, so building a policy
object there is cheap.

## 8. Reading a failure

`AuthorizationResult.Failure` carries two things worth having:

```csharp
var decision = await authorization.AuthorizeAsync(user, proposal, "DecideProposal");

if (!decision.Succeeded)
{
    var vetoes = decision.Failure!.FailureReasons.Select(r => r.Message);
    var pending = decision.Failure!.FailedRequirements.Select(r => r.GetType().Name);
}
```

`FailureReasons` holds what explicit `Fail(reason)` calls said — so it is empty
when the failure was simply "nobody succeeded". `FailedRequirements` holds the
requirements that were not satisfied. The difference matters when you build a
403 body: a caller who tripped a veto can be told what they tripped, while a
caller who merely did not qualify has nothing specific to be told, and
manufacturing a message for them will be wrong.

The same distinction shows up in `PolicyAuthorizationResult`, which the
authorization middleware produces: `Challenged` when no identity was established
and `Forbidden` when one was. Replacing
`IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler` lets you write a body for the second
without touching the first — the review exercise.

## 9. Testing policies without HTTP

Handlers are ordinary classes and can be exercised directly, which is the main
practical reason to prefer them over assertions:

```csharp
var requirement = new SeniorityRequirement(5);
var user = new ClaimsPrincipal(new ClaimsIdentity(
    [new Claim("grade", "7")], "test", "sub", "role"));
var context = new AuthorizationHandlerContext([requirement], user, resource: null);

await new SeniorityHandler().HandleAsync(context);

Assert.True(context.HasSucceeded);
```

No server, no token, no HTTP. A rule that can be tested this way is a rule whose
edge cases actually get tested, and every table of "grade 4, grade 5, grade 6,
no claim" is three lines each instead of a request each.

## 10. Choosing between 403 and 404

Once a resource-based check can refuse, you have a second decision: does the
caller learn that the resource exists?

```csharp
var proposal = board.Find(id);
if (proposal is null) return TypedResults.NotFound();

var decision = await authorization.AuthorizeAsync(user, proposal, "ReadProposal");
if (!decision.Succeeded)
    return hideExistence
        ? TypedResults.NotFound()
        : TypedResults.Forbid(authenticationSchemes: [V3DA04Jwt.Scheme]);
```

403 is the honest answer and the right default for an internal API: the caller
knows the id, and telling them "this exists and you may not see it" lets them ask
the right person for access. 404 is right when existence is itself the secret —
sequential ids that can be enumerated, or a resource whose presence discloses
something (a draft acquisition, a sealed complaint). The cost of 404 is a support
burden: legitimate callers who lost access see the same answer as callers who
typo'd an id, and cannot tell which happened.

Whichever you pick, pick it per *resource type* and write it down. An API where
some endpoints hide and others do not is one an attacker can use to map exactly
which resources are sensitive.

## 11. Common mistakes

1. **A resource-typed handler under `RequireAuthorization`.** Never runs; no
   error.
2. **Calling `Fail` when you merely cannot decide.** Vetoes your siblings.
3. **`Succeed(requirement)` with the wrong instance.** Satisfies a different
   requirement of the same type.
4. **Validating before authorizing.** Leaks field-level detail to callers with no
   access.
5. **Returning null from a custom `GetPolicyAsync` for unknown names.** Every
   registered policy stops working.
6. **Forgetting `AddAuthenticationSchemes` on a policy.** With no default scheme,
   the policy authenticates nobody and everything is a 401.
7. **Roles for everything.** A role is a claim with a helper; a rule about a pair
   of things is not expressible as one.
8. **403 where the resource is secret.** Confirms existence to someone who should
   not know.

## 12. The interview answer

> *"How would you implement 'a reviewer may read a proposal only if assigned to
> it and has no declared conflict'?"*

Not with roles — the rule is about a reviewer and a proposal together, so it
needs the proposal. I would define a `ProposalAccessRequirement`, an
`AssignmentHandler` typed `AuthorizationHandler<ProposalAccessRequirement,
Proposal>` that succeeds when the caller is in the proposal's reviewer list, and
a `ConflictHandler` on the same requirement that calls `Fail` when a conflict is
declared — because `Fail` beats any sibling success, which is exactly the
semantics "unless" needs. The endpoint loads the proposal, 404s when it does not
exist, then calls `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, proposal,
"ReadProposal")` and forbids on failure. It cannot be an endpoint-level policy,
because the middleware supplies the `HttpContext` as the resource and runs long
before the proposal is loaded.

## 13. Check yourself

1. State the relationship between policies, requirements and handlers in three
   sentences.
2. How do you express OR between two authorization rules?
3. What does `context.Fail()` do to a sibling handler's `Succeed`?
4. What is `context.Resource` under `RequireAuthorization`, and what follows?
5. Why does `AuthorizationHandler<TReq, TResource>` silently not run sometimes?
6. Write the call that authorizes against a loaded entity.
7. What is the difference between the default policy and the fallback policy?
8. What beats a fallback policy, and how is it implemented?
9. Why must a custom policy provider delegate unknown names?
10. When is `GetPolicyAsync` called, and how often?
11. Why should validation come after authorization in a write endpoint?
12. Give a case where 404 is the right answer for a resource that exists.
13. What is `AuthorizationFailureReason` for?

# Reading — the authorization system, and why it looks like this

## The problem with permission checks

Every application eventually grows a function called something like `CanEdit`.
It starts as a role check, gains an ownership check, then a special case for
administrators, then an exception for archived records, and after two years it is
four hundred lines called from thirty places, half of which pass slightly
different arguments. Nobody can say what the rules are without reading it, and
nobody dares change it.

The design ASP.NET Core lands on attacks that directly. A rule becomes an object.
Rules compose by a fixed algebra rather than by whatever `&&` and `||` the author
felt like. And the composition has a specific asymmetry — failure dominates —
which turns out to be what real policy documents look like: a list of ways to
qualify, plus a list of disqualifications that override them.

## What runs, and when

`AuthorizationMiddleware` runs after routing. It reads
`IAuthorizeData` metadata off the selected endpoint, asks
`IAuthorizationPolicyProvider` to turn the policy names into an
`AuthorizationPolicy`, and combines them with the fallback if there is no
metadata at all. Before any of that, it checks for `IAllowAnonymous` and skips
everything if present.

It then authenticates with the policy's schemes — note, *the policy's*, not the
default — merges the resulting principals, and calls
`IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, httpContext, policy)`. The
`HttpContext` as the resource is not an accident or a placeholder: it is the only
thing that exists at that point, and it is genuinely useful.

Finally it hands the result to `IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler`, whose
default implementation challenges when nothing authenticated and forbids
otherwise. Replacing that handler is how you customise the 403 body, and it is
also how features like "redirect to an upgrade page when the policy failed on a
subscription requirement" are built.

Requirement evaluation itself is `DefaultAuthorizationService` looping over every
registered `IAuthorizationHandler`. Note *every*: the handlers are not indexed by
requirement type, so a hundred registered handlers means a hundred calls per
authorization, each of which loops over the pending requirements looking for ones
it recognises. `AuthorizationHandler<T>`'s base implementation does that
filtering for you. The cost is small but not zero, and it is a reason to keep
handlers few and cohesive rather than writing one per rule variant.

## The `Fail` semantics, and the option that changes them

`AuthorizationHandlerContext.Fail()` sets a flag. `HasSucceeded` is
`!_failCalled && PendingRequirements.Count == 0`. That is the entire mechanism,
and it explains everything: a `Fail` anywhere is fatal, a `Succeed` only removes
one requirement from the pending set, and a requirement nobody handles remains
pending and therefore fails silently — which is worth remembering, because
forgetting to register a handler produces a 403 with no diagnostic at all.

`AuthorizationOptions.InvokeHandlersAfterFailure` defaults to `true`, so all
handlers run even after a failure. The reason is diagnostics: you get every
failure reason rather than the first. Setting it to `false` is a performance
choice for hot paths with expensive handlers, and it makes the result depend on
handler registration order, which is a subtle thing to introduce.

## Resource-based authorization, and the ordering it forces

The framework's split — declarative policies at the endpoint, imperative calls
for resources — annoys people who want one mechanism. But the split is forced by
time. An endpoint policy is evaluated before the handler runs, which is before
the database has been touched. Any rule that mentions a stored object therefore
cannot be an endpoint policy. There is no design that avoids this; frameworks
that appear to (by, say, letting an attribute name a repository method) have just
moved the loading into the authorization layer, where it is harder to see, harder
to cache, and duplicated with the load the handler is about to do anyway.

Accepting the split leads to a clean shape for a write endpoint:

1. load — 404 if absent;
2. authorize against the loaded thing — 403 (or 404, if existence is secret);
3. validate the payload — 400 or 422;
4. check state — 409;
5. do the work.

Each step needs the previous one. Reordering any pair produces either a leak or a
misleading error, and it is worth being able to say which for each pair.

## Dynamic policies

Permission systems tend to have hundreds of names, and registering hundreds of
`AddPolicy` calls is both tedious and a deployment coupling — a new permission
should not require a code change in the authorization setup. `IAuthorization
PolicyProvider` solves it by making the policy name a small DSL.

Two cautions. First, delegate: return the default provider's answer for names you
do not recognise, or you have silently deleted every conventional policy in the
application. Second, the provider is a singleton and `GetPolicyAsync` may be
called concurrently; building a fresh `AuthorizationPolicy` each time is cheap
and thread-safe, whereas a lazily-populated dictionary needs to actually be
concurrent.

The related pattern is a requirement carrying the parameter — a single
`PermissionRequirement(string permission)` with one handler — rather than a
requirement type per permission. That keeps handler count constant as permissions
grow, which matters given the loop described above.

## Where claims come from, and the thing that ruins this design

Everything here assumes the principal already carries what the rules need. When
it does not — when deciding requires a database lookup of the caller's
memberships — you have a choice, and both options have real costs.

Putting memberships in the token makes authorization a pure function of the
request, which is fast and cacheable, and makes revocation slow: a reviewer
removed from a panel keeps their access until the token expires. Looking
memberships up in a handler makes revocation instant and puts a query on every
authorized request, which then wants caching, which reintroduces staleness with
extra steps.

The usual resolution is by blast radius. Coarse, slow-changing facts — employment
status, tenant, broad role — go in the token with a short lifetime. Fine,
fast-changing facts — this specific assignment, this specific conflict — get
looked up, and are looked up anyway as part of loading the resource, so the
handler that receives the resource often already has what it needs. That is a
quiet third argument for resource-based handlers: the data is already in memory.

## When not to use this

**Do not use policies for business rules that are not about permission.** "A
proposal cannot be submitted after the deadline" is a 409 from your domain, not a
403 from authorization. The test is whether the answer changes with *who* is
asking. If it does not, it is not authorization.

**Do not use the authorization system for row filtering.** Deciding whether a
caller may see one proposal is authorization; producing the list of proposals
they may see is a query. Running an authorization check per row is how a list
endpoint gets slow, and it produces the wrong pagination besides.

**Do not put expensive work in a handler that runs on every request.** Handlers
are called for every requirement evaluation on every request to a protected
endpoint. A handler that calls a service is a per-request dependency on that
service's availability.

## Further reading

- [Policy-based authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/policies)
- [Resource-based authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/resourcebased)
- [Custom authorization policy providers](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/iauthorizationpolicyprovider)
- [Claims-based authorization](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/claims)
- [Authorization middleware result handler](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/authorization/authorizationmiddlewareresulthandler)

## Exercise 1 — a policy is a list of requirements, all of which must hold

Edit `src/Api/V3DA04_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex1.cs`, `Ex1Services` only — the
endpoints are given and correct.

The board data is at the bottom of the file: four proposals across panels
`bio` and `phys`, reviewers `rlee`, `mokafor` and `dchan`, and a `chair` role.
The bearer scheme `V3DA04Jwt.Scheme` is given and correct; by the time any policy
here runs, the token is already valid and its claims are `sub`, `role`, `panel`
and `grade`.

Register a policy named `V3DA04Policies.PanelMember` that admits a caller who is
authenticated **and** carries a `panel` claim, under that scheme.

`GET /v3da04/proposals` is already mapped with
`.RequireAuthorization(V3DA04Policies.PanelMember)` and returns every proposal,
id ascending, as `{"id","title","panel","state"}`.

Expected:

- no token → **401**, with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`
- a valid token with **no `panel` claim** → **403**, no `WWW-Authenticate`
- a valid token with `panel=bio` → **200** with all four proposals

The 403 is the thing to look at. Two requirements, both mandatory; the caller
satisfied the first and not the second, so authorization failed, and because an
identity *was* established the middleware forbids rather than challenges. There
is no `.Or(...)` on the builder and you should not look for one — every clause
you chain narrows the policy.

Note `AddAuthenticationSchemes` on the policy. Nothing in this sector sets a
default scheme, so a policy that does not name one authenticates nobody and every
request is a 401 — a failure that looks exactly like a missing token.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da04_authorization_policies ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the policy builder as a conjunction. Each `Require…` call appends a
requirement, and the policy succeeds only when every one of them is satisfied.

## Hint 2

The same shape for a different claim:

    services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
        .AddPolicy("Auditor", policy => policy
            .AddAuthenticationSchemes(SchemeName)
            .RequireAuthenticatedUser()
            .RequireClaim("audit"));

`RequireClaim("x")` asserts presence of a claim of that type;
`RequireClaim("x", "a", "b")` additionally restricts its value.

## Hint 3

Three chained calls and a policy name from `V3DA04Policies`. The decision left to
you: `RequireClaim("panel")` or `RequireClaim("panel", "bio", "phys")`? One of
them keeps working when a third panel is created and the other does not — say
which behaviour you want and why.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Get the two failure responses side by side before anything else. `curl -i` with
no token and with a panel-less token: same endpoint, same policy, different
status and a header present in one and absent in the other. That difference is
the entire 401/403 rule made visible.

## Hint 2

If the panel-less token gets **401** instead of 403, the policy did not name a
scheme — authentication never ran, so no identity existed, so the middleware
challenged. This is the single most common misconfiguration in a multi-scheme
application and it looks identical to a missing token from the client's side.

## Hint 3

Notice that the endpoint returns *every* proposal, including the `phys` ones, to
a `bio` caller. That is deliberate: this policy says who may call the endpoint,
not what they may see. Row filtering is a query concern, and conflating the two
is how a list endpoint becomes slow and paginates wrongly — the reading has more
on why.

## Exercise 2 — a rule that has to look at the request

Edit `src/Api/V3DA04_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex2.cs`, `Ex2Services` only.

`GET /v3da04/panels/{panel}/proposals` returns that panel's proposals, id
ascending. The rule: a caller may read a panel when it is **their own** panel, or
when they are the chair. The panel being asked about is a route value, so no
claim comparison alone can express it.

Register `V3DA04Policies.OwnPanel` using `RequireAssertion`. Inside the
assertion, `context.Resource` is the `HttpContext` — that is what the
authorization middleware supplies — so read
`http.Request.RouteValues["panel"]` and compare it with the caller's `panel`
claim, ordinally, or accept the caller outright when they are in role `chair`.

Expected, for `/v3da04/panels/bio/proposals`:

- no token → 401
- `panel=bio` → **200** with proposals 1 and 3
- `panel=phys` → **403**

## Exercise 3 — a requirement carries the parameters, a handler carries the logic

Edit `src/Api/V3DA04_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex3.cs`.

`SeniorityRequirement` is given:

```csharp
public class SeniorityRequirement(int minimum) : IAuthorizationRequirement
{
    public int Minimum { get; } = minimum;
}
```

The policy `V3DA04Policies.Senior` is registered with
`.AddRequirements(new SeniorityRequirement(5))` and there is no handler, so the
requirement stays pending and every caller is refused. Write
`SeniorityHandler : AuthorizationHandler<SeniorityRequirement>` and register it,
so the requirement is satisfied when the caller's `grade` claim is **at least
`requirement.Minimum`**. `V3DA04Claims.GradeOf(user)` is given and returns 0 for
a caller with no `grade` claim or an unparseable one. A grade of exactly 5 passes
a minimum of 5.

`GET /v3da04/proposals/scored` is mapped with that policy and returns the
proposals whose `State` is `scored`, id ascending.

Expected: no token → 401; `grade=3` → 403; `grade=5` → 200; `grade=9` → 200; no
`grade` claim → 403.

Two details that are the exercise rather than incidental.

The bound comes from the **requirement**, not from a constant in the handler.
That is the split the design is built on: one handler serves
`new SeniorityRequirement(5)` and `new SeniorityRequirement(8)` and any other
configured instance, and the number lives with the policy that chose it.

`context.Succeed(requirement)` takes the **instance** the context handed you, not
the type. When a policy carries two `SeniorityRequirement`s with different
minimums — unusual but legal — succeeding one must not satisfy the other.

And do not call `Fail` when the grade is too low. A handler that cannot say yes
should say nothing; failing here would veto the second handler you are about to
write in ex4.

```

```

## Exercise 4 — two handlers, one requirement, and that is your OR

Edit `src/Api/V3DA04_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex4.cs`.

A **panel lead** is somebody at grade 8 or above, **or** the chair, regardless of
grade. `PanelLeadRequirement` is given and empty, the policy
`V3DA04Policies.PanelLead` is registered with it, and
`PanelLeadByGradeHandler` is given and correct — it succeeds at grade 8 or above.

Write `PanelLeadByRoleHandler` and register it, as a **second handler on the same
requirement**, not as an extra `||` inside the first.

`GET /v3da04/panels/leads` is mapped with the policy and returns the distinct
panel names, alphabetically: `{"panels":["bio","phys"]}`.

Expected: `grade=9` → 200; `grade=2, role=chair` → 200; `grade=2` → 403;
`grade=9, role=chair` → 200; no token → 401.

Why a second handler rather than a second clause. Each reason to say yes is a
separately named class, so "why can the chair do this" is answerable by finding
one file. Each is separately testable without constructing the other's inputs.
And adding a third route to leadership later — an explicit `lead` claim, say —
touches no existing file, which means no chance of breaking the two rules that
already work.

The two handlers are unordered. Both run, either can succeed, and neither knows
the other exists. If you find yourself wanting one to run first, or to know what
the other decided, the rule you are modelling is probably not an OR — and the
requirement should be split.

Neither handler calls `Fail`. That is not an oversight: a grade-2 non-chair is
refused because the requirement was never satisfied, not because anyone vetoed
it. The difference becomes visible in ex6.

```

```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — the decision needs the thing being decided about

Edit `src/Api/V3DA04_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex5.cs`.

`PUT /v3da04/proposals/{id:int}/score` takes `record ScoreChange(int Score)` and
must behave in exactly this order:

1. no such proposal → **404**
2. `V3DA04Policies.ScoreProposal` refuses this caller **for this proposal** →
   **403**
3. `score` outside 0 to 10 → **400** validation problem keyed `"score"`
4. otherwise **204**, with the score written

Fill in `ReviewerAssignmentHandler : AuthorizationHandler<ProposalAccessRequirement,
Proposal>`: succeed when the caller's `sub` is in `resource.Reviewers`, or when
the caller is in role `chair`. Then call, from the endpoint:

```csharp
var decision = await authorization.AuthorizeAsync(user, proposal, V3DA04Policies.ScoreProposal);
```

and forbid when it fails. `IAuthorizationService` is injected as a handler
parameter.

Expected: proposal 1's reviewers are `rlee` and `mokafor`. `sub=rlee` → 204;
`sub=dchan` → 403; `sub=dchan, role=chair` → 204; `id=99` → 404 for everybody,
including `dchan`; `sub=rlee` with `score=20` → 400 keyed `score`.

The structural point: `V3DA04Policies.ScoreProposal` is **never** used with
`RequireAuthorization`. Under the middleware, `context.Resource` is the
`HttpContext`, so a handler typed on `Proposal` would be filtered out by its own
base class and never run — silently, with no error, producing an endpoint that
403s everybody because the requirement stayed pending.

The ordering is graded and each step needs the one before it. 404 first, because
there is nothing to authorize against. Authorization before validation, because
telling a caller with no rights which of their fields were malformed is a small
leak and a large annoyance.

`TypedResults.Forbid(authenticationSchemes: [V3DA04Jwt.Scheme])` is the forbid
that goes through the scheme, rather than a hand-written 403.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da04_authorization_policies ex5
```

## Exercise 6 — a handler that says no and means it

Edit `src/Api/V3DA04_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex6.cs`.

`DELETE /v3da04/proposals/{id:int}/reviews/{reviewer}` is given and correct: 404
for an unknown proposal or reviewer, 403 when
`V3DA04Policies.RemoveReview` refuses, otherwise 204.

`ReviewRemovalHandler` is given and correct: the chair, **or** the reviewer
removing their own review, may do it.

Write `ConflictOfInterestHandler : AuthorizationHandler<ReviewRemovalRequirement,
Proposal>` so that a proposal with a **declared conflict** for the calling
reviewer can never have reviews removed — by anybody, including the chair, whose
handler has already succeeded on that same requirement.

`proposal.Conflicts` is a `HashSet<string>` of reviewer subjects. The rule: if
the *calling* reviewer's `sub` is in `Conflicts`, refuse. Call
`context.Fail(new AuthorizationFailureReason(this, "A conflict of interest is
declared."))` rather than bare `Fail()`.

Then set `AuthorizationOptions.InvokeHandlersAfterFailure = false` in
`Ex6Services` and map `GET /v3da04/proposals/{id:int}/handlers` returning
`{"ran":n}` from a static counter that both handlers increment.

Expected, with proposal 2 having a conflict declared for `dchan`:

- `sub=dchan` on proposal 2 → **403**, even though `dchan` owns the review
- `sub=rlee, role=chair` on proposal 2 → **204**, because the conflict is
  `dchan`'s, not theirs
- `sub=dchan` on proposal 1, which has no conflicts → **204**
- with a conflicting caller, `/handlers` shows fewer runs than without

Two things. A veto is the only way to express "unless" without editing every
other handler — and the day somebody adds a fourth reason to say yes and forgets
about conflicts is the day the veto proves its worth. And
`InvokeHandlersAfterFailure = false` stops evaluation at the first failure, which
is cheaper and loses the ability to collect *every* reason a request was refused;
that trade is worth making deliberately rather than by default.

```

```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — closed by default, open on purpose

Edit `src/Api/V3DA04_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex7.cs`.

Set a **fallback policy** in `Ex7Services` requiring an authenticated user under
`V3DA04Jwt.Scheme`, and a **default policy** additionally requiring a `panel`
claim. Then map five endpoints under `/v3da04/guard`, each demonstrating one rule
of the interaction:

- `GET /v3da04/guard/implicit` — **no** authorization call at all. Returns
  `{"guard":"implicit"}`. Protected by the fallback policy: no token → 401, any
  valid token → 200, panel claim irrelevant.
- `GET /v3da04/guard/default` — `.RequireAuthorization()` with no arguments.
  Protected by the **default** policy: a token with no `panel` claim → 403.
- `GET /v3da04/guard/named` — `.RequireAuthorization(V3DA04Policies.Senior)`.
  Neither fallback nor default applies; only the named policy does.
- `GET /v3da04/guard/open` — `.AllowAnonymous()`. Returns 200 with **no** token,
  despite the fallback policy.
- `GET /v3da04/guard/contradiction` — both `.RequireAuthorization()` **and**
  `.AllowAnonymous()`. Returns 200 with no token, because `AllowAnonymous` wins.

Expected grid, with no token: `implicit` 401, `default` 401, `named` 401, `open`
200, `contradiction` 200. With a valid token carrying no `panel` claim and
`grade=1`: `implicit` 200, `default` 403, `named` 403.

The fallback policy is the point. Without one, an endpoint somebody forgot to
protect is open, and nothing anywhere reports it — the failure is an absence.
With one, forgetting produces a 401 in the first test that touches the endpoint,
and *opening* something requires writing `AllowAnonymous`, which is a line a
reviewer can see in a diff.

The contradiction endpoint is not a trick question. `AllowAnonymous` is metadata
the middleware checks *before* evaluating anything, and it wins unconditionally —
over group policies, over the fallback, over an `[Authorize]` on the same
endpoint. That is what makes it a usable opt-out and also what makes an
accidental one dangerous.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da04_authorization_policies ex7
```

## Exercise 8 — policies built from their own names

Edit `src/Api/V3DA04_AuthorizationPolicies/Ex8.cs`.

The board has grown a permission model: callers carry zero or more `perm` claims
like `proposal.read`, `proposal.score` and `panel.manage`, and endpoints want to
say `.RequireAuthorization("permission:proposal.score")` without somebody
registering a policy per permission.

Write `PermissionPolicyProvider : IAuthorizationPolicyProvider`:

- `GetPolicyAsync(name)` — for a name starting `permission:`, build and return an
  `AuthorizationPolicy` requiring `V3DA04Jwt.Scheme`, an authenticated user, and
  a `perm` claim whose value is the rest of the name. For anything else,
  **delegate** to a `DefaultAuthorizationPolicyProvider` you construct from
  `IOptions<AuthorizationOptions>`.
- `GetDefaultPolicyAsync()` and `GetFallbackPolicyAsync()` — delegate.

Register it with `services.AddSingleton<IAuthorizationPolicyProvider,
PermissionPolicyProvider>()`, and keep the ordinary `V3DA04Policies.PanelMember`
policy registered too, so you can prove delegation works.

Map three endpoints:

- `GET /v3da04/perm/read` — `.RequireAuthorization("permission:proposal.read")`
- `POST /v3da04/perm/score/{id:int}` —
  `.RequireAuthorization("permission:proposal.score")`, 404 for an unknown
  proposal, else 204
- `GET /v3da04/perm/panel` — `.RequireAuthorization(V3DA04Policies.PanelMember)`,
  which must still work

Also map `GET /v3da04/perm/built` returning `{"built":n}`, a static counter
incremented each time your provider **builds** a permission policy.

Expected: a token with `perm=proposal.read` gets 200 on `/read` and 403 on
`/score/1`; a token with both permissions gets 200 and 204; a token with a
`panel` claim and no `perm` gets 200 on `/panel` and 403 on `/read`. And
`/built` stops increasing after the first request to each endpoint, because the
middleware caches the policy per endpoint.

Two traps live here. Returning `null` from `GetPolicyAsync` for an unrecognised
name deletes every conventional policy in the application, so `/panel` breaks and
the cause is nowhere near the symptom. And the provider is a **singleton** whose
methods may be called concurrently — building a fresh policy each time is cheap
and safe, while a lazily-populated `Dictionary` is a race.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da04_authorization_policies ex8
```

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a dynamic policy, a loaded resource, and a veto

Honest difficulty note: each mechanism is one you have already built. The
difficulty is that two of them cannot be combined the obvious way — a
permission-name policy is evaluated by the middleware, and a resource handler is
not — so you have to decide which check happens where.

Edit `src/Api/V3DA04_AuthorizationPolicies/Challenge.cs`.

`POST /v3da04/board/proposals/{id:int}/decision` takes
`record Decision(string Outcome, string? Note)` and must behave in this order:

1. the endpoint carries `.RequireAuthorization("permission:proposal.decide")`, so
   a caller without that `perm` claim is refused by the **middleware** — 401 with
   no token, 403 with a token lacking the permission
2. no such proposal → **404**
3. `V3DA04Policies.DecideProposal`, evaluated against the loaded proposal, refuses
   → **403** problem, `title` = `Not permitted`, extension `reasons` carrying
   every `AuthorizationFailureReason.Message`, ordinally ordered
4. `outcome` not one of `fund`, `reject`, `defer` → **422** validation problem
   keyed `"outcome"`
5. the proposal is already decided → **409** problem, `title` = `Already
   decided`
6. otherwise **200** `{"id":n,"outcome":"fund","decidedBy":"<sub>"}`

`V3DA04Policies.DecideProposal` carries one `DecisionRequirement` with **three**
handlers:

- `PanelChairHandler` — succeeds when the caller is in role `chair` **and** their
  `panel` claim equals `proposal.Panel`
- `DelegatedDeciderHandler` — succeeds when the caller's `sub` is in
  `proposal.Deciders`
- `SealedProposalHandler` — **fails**, with the reason `The proposal is sealed.`,
  when `proposal.Sealed` is true

Leave `InvokeHandlersAfterFailure` at its default `true`, so that a sealed
proposal that the caller *also* had no route to decide produces two reasons.

The gate's sequence:

1. no token → 401
2. token with `perm=proposal.read` only → 403 from the middleware, and the
   response body must **not** contain a `reasons` extension — the resource check
   never ran
3. `perm=proposal.decide`, unknown proposal id → 404
4. `perm=proposal.decide`, `sub=dchan`, proposal 1 (deciders `rlee`) → 403 with
   `reasons` present and empty
5. `perm=proposal.decide`, `role=chair, panel=phys`, proposal 1 (panel `bio`) →
   403
6. `perm=proposal.decide`, `sub=rlee`, proposal 3, which is sealed → 403 with
   `reasons` containing `The proposal is sealed.`
7. `perm=proposal.decide`, `sub=rlee`, proposal 1, `outcome=maybe` → 422
8. same with `outcome=fund` → 200, and again → 409

Step 2 versus step 4 is the design decision worth defending: a caller with no
permission at all learns only that they were refused, while a caller with the
permission who failed a resource rule learns why. Disclosure grows with
established access.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da04_authorization_policies challenge
```
