exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write out, for each of the eight steps, which of the two authorization checks
runs and what the answer is. Steps 2 and 4 both produce 403 through completely
different code paths, and confusing them is what makes the `reasons` assertion
fail in a way that looks like a serialisation bug.

## Hint 2

If step 6 shows an empty `reasons` array, your seal handler is not running — most
likely typed without the resource, so it never receives a `Proposal`. If it shows
the reason but the request succeeds, you called `Fail` on a different requirement
instance than the one in the context.

## Hint 3

Try flipping `InvokeHandlersAfterFailure` to `false` and re-running step 6 with a
caller who is also not a decider. With early exit you may see one reason or none
depending on the order the container returns the handlers — and the container's
order is registration order, which nobody thinks of as part of an API's contract.
That fragility is the price of the optimisation, and it is why the default is the
slower, complete answer.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — deciding what a 403 says

`review1` is not part of finishing this sector; the scheduler brings it back
later.

Edit `src/Api/V3DA04_AuthorizationPolicies/Review1.cs`. By default the
authorization middleware writes a 403 with an **empty body**, which tells an
integrator nothing. Replace that.

Implement `BoardAuthorizationResultHandler : IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler`
wrapping the built-in `AuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler`:

- `authorizeResult.Challenged` → delegate to the inner handler untouched, so the
  scheme still writes its own 401 and `WWW-Authenticate`
- `authorizeResult.Forbidden` → write a **403** `application/problem+json` with
  `title` = `Not permitted`, `status` = 403, an extension `policy` naming the
  failed policy from `HttpContext.GetEndpoint()`'s
  `IAuthorizeData` metadata (first non-null `Policy`, or `"default"`), and an
  extension `requirements` listing the **type names** of
  `authorizeResult.Failure!.FailedRequirements`, ordinally ordered
- anything else → delegate

Register with `services.AddSingleton<IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler,
BoardAuthorizationResultHandler>()` — a single registration replaces the default,
which is why it must delegate for the cases it does not handle.

Map `GET /v3da04/report/proposals` with
`.RequireAuthorization(V3DA04Policies.Senior)` (minimum grade 5) returning the
proposals, and `GET /v3da04/report/open` with `.AllowAnonymous()`.

Expected: no token → 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` and no problem body;
`grade=1` → 403 with `{"title":"Not permitted","status":403,"policy":"...",
"requirements":["SeniorityRequirement"]}`; `grade=7` → 200; `/open` → 200 with no
token.

Now the judgement, which is the same one as DA3's `error_description` and worth
meeting twice. Naming the failed requirement type is genuinely useful to a
partner integrating against you: `SeniorityRequirement` tells them to ask for a
higher grade rather than to file a ticket. It also tells anyone probing your API
the internal names of your authorization rules, and a requirement called
`InternalStaffOnlyRequirement` leaks more than it helps.

The workable middle ground in production is a stable, curated code — `insufficient
_grade` — mapped from the requirement type, so the client gets something
actionable and documented and you keep the freedom to rename the class. Implement
the type-name version here because it is what the gate can check, and know that
it is the prototype rather than the shipping design.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da04_authorization_policies review1
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Confirm the 401 path first. If your handler intercepts challenges as well as
forbids, you will have replaced the bearer scheme's `WWW-Authenticate` with a
problem document, and a client that reads that header to decide how to
authenticate now has nothing to read.

## Hint 2

If the success path stops working — every request 404s or hangs — you forgot to
`await next(http)` (or to delegate to the inner handler) when the result was
neither challenged nor forbidden. This service is in the request path, not beside
it: not calling `next` is not calling the endpoint.

## Hint 3

Write the curated-code version on paper even though the gate wants type names: a
`Dictionary<Type, string>` from requirement type to a documented code, with an
`unknown` fallback. Then ask what happens when a requirement has no entry — do
you leak the type name, or say nothing? Choosing "say nothing, and log that the
mapping is missing" is the answer that stays safe as the codebase grows, and it
is the kind of default worth building in from the start.

lessons.title: V3·DA5 — API versioning and evolving a contract
lessons.summary: Versioning is the part of API design where you find out how honest your abstractions were. This sector builds three version selectors, adds fields without breaking anyone, retires a version through deprecation headers and a 410, and settles which changes need a new version at all.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·DA5 — API versioning and evolving a contract

Every endpoint you have written so far in this volume has one thing in common:
exactly one client, which you also wrote, and which you can change at the same
time as the server. That is the situation in which versioning is unnecessary and
therefore invisible. This sector is about the other situation — the one that
starts the day somebody else's code depends on your JSON, and never ends.

The first thing to internalise is that versioning is not a feature you add. It is
a set of costs you choose between. Every version you support is a code path you
maintain, a test matrix column, and a set of behaviours you cannot fix. Every
version you *do not* support is an integrator whose build broke. The whole
subject is about paying as little as possible of both.

## Concept — most changes do not need a version

Before any machinery, the taxonomy, because it decides everything else.

**Additive changes are usually safe.** A new field in a response, a new optional
field in a request, a new endpoint, a new enum value in a field the client
filters on rather than switches over. These are safe *if* clients are tolerant
readers — if they ignore fields they do not recognise. Most JSON clients are,
because most deserialisers ignore unknown properties by default. This is why
"add a field" is not a breaking change and "rename a field" is.

**Breaking changes need a version.** Removing or renaming a field. Changing a
type — `"quantity": 4` to `"quantity": "4"`, or an integer id to a string.
Changing the meaning of a value while keeping its name. Making an optional
request field required. Tightening validation so previously accepted input is
refused. Changing a status code for an existing condition.

**The sneaky ones.** Changing a default. Changing sort order when clients relied
on it. Adding a required header. Making a synchronous operation asynchronous.
Reducing a page's maximum size. None of these look like contract changes in a
diff and all of them break somebody.

The engineering discipline that saves the most versions is being ruthless about
the first category: design responses so that adding to them is natural, and never
put information in a *shape* when it could be in a field.

## Concept — three places to put the version

**In the path.** `/v3da05/v1/quotes`, `/v3da05/v2/quotes`. Explicit, visible in
logs and in a browser, trivially cacheable, and impossible to get wrong by
accident. The purist objection is that a URL should identify a resource and
`/v1/quotes` and `/v2/quotes` are the same resource; the practical answer is that
every large public API does this anyway, because a URL you can paste into a bug
report is worth more than URI purity.

**In a header or query string.** `X-Api-Version: 2`, or `?api-version=2`. Keeps
one URL per resource. Invisible in logs unless you add it, easy to forget, and
caches need to be told to vary on it. The query-string form is a decent
compromise: visible and pasteable, and does not change the path.

**In the media type.** `Accept: application/json; v=2`, or a vendor type like
`application/vnd.freight.quote.v2+json`. The most correct by HTTP's own model —
you are negotiating a representation, which is exactly what `Accept` is for — and
the most awkward for everybody: hard to type, hard to debug, and requires clients
to build `Accept` headers deliberately.

Real APIs pick one and support a second grudgingly. What matters more than the
choice is that **unversioned requests have a defined answer**, and that the
answer is written down. Defaulting to the latest version means your API breaks
lazy clients on every release; defaulting to the oldest means new clients silently
get old behaviour. Defaulting to a refusal — 400, "state a version" — is the
strictest and the kindest, and is unpopular because it breaks the first `curl`
anyone tries.

## Concept — one implementation, several shapes

The mistake that makes versioning expensive is duplicating handlers. Two copies
of a quote calculation diverge within a quarter, and then a bug is fixed in one.

The shape that survives is a single implementation over a current domain model,
plus a thin **adapter per version** that maps that model to the shape that
version promised. Adapters are small, pure, individually testable, and — the
important part — the only place a version's peculiarities live. When v1 is
retired, you delete one file.

That leaves one hard case: a version whose *behaviour* differs, not just its
shape. v1 rounds down and v2 rounds to nearest. There is no adapter for that, and
the honest answers are a parameter threaded through the domain, or accepting that
you must keep two code paths and marking them loudly.

## What this sector drills

The domain is a **freight rate quoting API** under `/v3da05/...`: lanes, quotes
and surcharges. It is a good domain for this because a quote is a money-shaped
object, and money-shaped objects are where contract changes hurt.

Exercise 1 does path versioning with shared handlers. Exercise 2 builds a header-
and-query selector with a precedence rule and a proper 400 for unsupported
versions. Exercise 3 does media-type versioning and its 406. Exercise 4 proves
that an additive change reaches new clients without disturbing old ones.

Exercise 5 is the adapter pattern: one domain object, two response shapes.
Exercise 6 signals deprecation with `Deprecation`, `Sunset` and `Link` headers.
Exercise 7 retires a version with a 410 that names its successor. Exercise 8
settles the default-version question by implementing all three policies and
comparing them.

The challenge runs three live versions of one endpoint through adapters with
stable error contracts. The review comes at evolution from the enum-and-error-code
angle, which is where tolerant reading is hardest.

A note on tooling. This sector builds the mechanisms by hand, because doing so
once makes the libraries legible. In production you would usually reach for
`Asp.Versioning.Http`, which gives you version sets, `HasApiVersion`,
`MapToApiVersion`, several readers, and an `api-supported-versions` response
header. It is a good library. It is also a thin layer over the ideas you are
about to write, and it cannot make the taxonomy decisions for you.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - dotnet/v3da05_api_versioning

## Notes

**Tolerant reading is the load-bearing assumption.** Everything about "additive
is safe" depends on clients ignoring unknown fields. `System.Text.Json` does by
default; `JsonSerializerOptions.UnmappedMemberHandling = Disallow` turns it off,
and a client that sets it has opted into breaking on your next release. Say so in
your documentation: "clients must ignore unknown members" is part of the
contract, and it is the sentence that buys you additive changes.

**Path versioning composes with route groups.** `app.MapGroup("/v3da05/v1")` and
`MapGroup("/v3da05/v2")`, with the same handler method mapped into both where the
shape has not changed, is the cheapest correct implementation. The group is also
where a version's deprecation headers and conventions belong.

**A version selector is an endpoint filter or middleware.** Header and query
versioning needs the version resolved *before* the handler and made available to
it. `HttpContext.Items` carries it; a filter is the natural place to read,
validate and store it, because a filter can refuse.

**Precedence must be defined, not emergent.** When a request carries both
`X-Api-Version: 1` and `?api-version=2`, something must win, and "whichever my
code checks first" is not a specification. Pick one, document it, and — the part
people skip — decide whether a *conflict* is a 400. Refusing contradictory input
is usually right, because a client sending both is a client with a bug.

**Media-type versioning uses parameters, not new types.** `application/json; v=2`
keeps the base type parseable by anything; `application/vnd.x.v2+json` does not.
The `+json` suffix exists to tell generic tooling it is still JSON, and half the
tooling ignores it.

**Deprecation has standard headers.** RFC 9745 defines `Deprecation` as a
Date-typed field and RFC 8594 defines `Sunset` as an HTTP-date after which the
resource is expected to stop working, plus a `Link` with `rel="sunset"` or
`rel="deprecation"` pointing at documentation. Using the standard names means
gateways and client libraries can surface them automatically.

**410 is for gone, 404 is for never was.** A retired version should answer 410
Gone with a problem document naming its successor, not 404. The difference is
actionable: 404 makes a client check their URL, 410 tells them to upgrade.

**Cache keys must include the version.** A response that varies by
`X-Api-Version` must send `Vary: X-Api-Version`, or a shared cache will serve v2
JSON to a v1 client. Path versioning avoids this entirely, which is one of its
best arguments.

**Version the payload, not the error contract.** A client's error handling should
survive an upgrade. If v1 returns a problem document with an `errors` dictionary
and v3 returns something else, an integrator moving between them rewrites code
that had nothing to do with the change they wanted. Keep `title`, `status`,
`errors` and your extension names identical across every version, and put the
version itself in an extension so a support conversation can start from the
response.

**Tag every version group.** `WithTags("v3da05-v1")` costs one call and is what
lets a document generator emit one OpenAPI document per version — the subject of
the next sector. An API with three live versions and one combined document
produces generated clients containing every version's methods side by side,
which defeats the purpose.

**Instrument version usage from day one.** The question that decides whether a
version can be retired is "who is still calling it", and it is unanswerable
retroactively. A counter keyed by version and caller — the API key or `sub` from
DA3 — costs nothing and is the difference between a sunset date you enforce and
one you keep postponing.

## ex1 - two groups, one handler

The v1 and v2 quote listings differ in one field name, so v2 gets its own
projection and everything else is shared. Notice how little code the second
version costs when the domain model is the thing you compute and the DTO is the
thing you version.

## ex2 - resolving a version from the request

The filter reads the header, then the query, refuses a conflict, applies the
default, and rejects anything unsupported with a 400 whose body lists the
versions that exist. That list is the difference between a client fixing their
call in a minute and filing a ticket.

## ex3 - negotiating a representation

`Accept: application/json; v=2` is parsed with `MediaTypeHeaderValue`, not with
string splitting, because quality values and multiple candidates are real. An
unsupported version here is a **406**, not a 400: the client asked for a
representation you cannot produce, which is precisely what 406 means.

## ex4 - adding without breaking

The new `surchargeTotal` field appears in both versions and the v1 client's
assertion set still passes. That is the whole demonstration, and it is worth
doing once with your own eyes, because "additive is safe" is the kind of claim
that feels risky until you have watched it not break anything.

## ex5 - the adapter

One `Quote`, two DTOs, two mapping functions, one handler. The alternative —
`if (version == 1) { … } else { … }` inside the handler — works for two versions
and collapses at three.

## ex6 - saying goodbye politely

`Deprecation`, `Sunset` and `Link` on every v1 response, applied as a group
convention so no endpoint can forget. The `Warning` header is the legacy
equivalent and is deprecated itself, which is a pleasing irony.

## ex7 - the 410

Retiring v1 means replacing its handlers with one that answers 410 for every path
under it, naming the successor. Keeping the route registered is the point: an
unregistered route gives 404 and tells the client nothing.

## ex8 - what an unversioned request gets

Three policies, three behaviours, one endpoint that reports which was applied.
Implementing all three is how you stop having an opinion and start having a
reason.

## challenge - three live versions

Adapters, deprecation on the oldest, a stable error contract across all of them.

## review1 - enums and error codes

The hardest thing to evolve is a closed set. A client that `switch`es over your
status values breaks when you add one, and there is no version bump that helps a
client which already shipped.

## Further reading

- [ASP.NET Core API versioning (Asp.Versioning)](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnet-api-versioning)
- [RFC 8594 — The Sunset HTTP Header Field](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8594)
- [RFC 9110 §15.5.11 — 410 Gone](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#name-410-gone)
- [System.Text.Json unmapped member handling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/serialization/system-text-json/missing-members)
- [Microsoft REST API guidelines — versioning](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines)
lessons.fullReading:
# Reading — evolving a contract you no longer control

## The asymmetry that makes this hard

Deploying a server change is one action. Getting every client to change is a
campaign — and for a public API it is not even possible, because you do not know
who they are. That asymmetry is the entire reason versioning exists, and it has a
corollary worth stating plainly: **you cannot fix a client that has already
shipped.** Every mechanism in this sector is about limiting how often you need
to.

Which is why the taxonomy comes before the machinery. A team that is disciplined
about additive change may go years on one version. A team that renames fields
whenever a better name occurs to them will be running four versions by the end of
the year, and the versioning framework will not have helped — it will just have
made the cost payable in smaller instalments.

## Tolerant readers, and where the assumption fails

"Additive is safe" rests entirely on Postel-style tolerant reading: clients
ignore what they do not understand. `System.Text.Json` ignores unknown properties
by default, as do Jackson, `encoding/json` and most others. So in practice the
assumption usually holds.

It fails in three specific places, and they are worth knowing because they are
where "we only added a field" incidents come from.

**Strict deserialisers.** A client that set
`UnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow`, or generated a schema-validating parser with
`additionalProperties: false`, will throw on your new field. This is why an API's
documentation should state that clients must ignore unknown members: it makes the
strict client's breakage their decision rather than your regression.

**Generated clients over a schema.** If you publish an OpenAPI document and a
client generates code from it, adding a field is fine, but adding an enum value
is often not — many generators produce a closed C# or TypeScript enum, and an
unknown value becomes a deserialisation error rather than a default. Enum
evolution is genuinely the hardest part of API evolution, and the mitigations are
all somewhat sad: model open sets as strings, document that unknown values must
be tolerated, or accept that new values need a version.

**Exhaustive switches.** Even with a tolerant deserialiser, a client that
`switch`es over your `status` values with no default arm will crash on a new one.
You cannot detect this from the wire, which is why "we may add values" belongs in
the documentation next to every open set.

## Why path versioning wins in practice

The REST-purist argument against `/v2/quotes` is real: the version is not part of
the resource's identity, and two URLs now name the same thing. The argument for
it is a pile of small operational facts that add up.

A version in the path is visible in every access log, so "how much traffic is
still on v1" is a log query rather than an instrumentation project. It is
pasteable — a bug report containing a URL is reproducible. It is cacheable
without `Vary`, which means CDNs and proxies do the right thing with no
configuration, and `Vary` on a custom header is the single most common cause of
cross-version cache poisoning. It cannot be lost by a client library that strips
unknown headers, or by a proxy that normalises them.

Header versioning's advantages are mostly aesthetic, and its one real advantage —
one URL per resource, so links and bookmarks survive a version bump — matters far
more for hypermedia APIs than for the JSON-over-HTTP that most of us write.

Media-type versioning is the most defensible under HTTP's own model and the least
used, for a simple reason: `curl` becomes `curl -H 'Accept: application/json;
v=2'`, and a scheme that makes the simplest possible request harder loses.

## Where versions cost the most

The naive picture of versioning cost is "two response shapes". The real costs are
elsewhere.

**Behavioural divergence.** Shapes are adaptable; behaviour is not. When v1
rounds down and v2 rounds to nearest, no adapter helps, and you are maintaining
two calculations that must both stay correct. The mitigation is to thread the
behavioural difference into the domain as an explicit parameter — a
`RoundingMode` on the quote request — so that the difference is one visible
argument rather than two forked code paths.

**Storage.** A version that promised a field you no longer compute forces you to
keep computing it, or to store it. That is how a retired concept survives in a
schema for years.

**Testing.** Every version multiplies the integration matrix. Contract tests per
version, run on every change, are the only thing that keeps this honest, and they
are also the thing that makes retiring a version safe.

**Support.** Two versions means every incoming question starts with "which
version are you on", and the answer is often wrong.

Those costs are why the lifecycle matters as much as the mechanism. A version you
never retire is a version you pay for forever, and the retirement has to be
planned when the version is created: publish a sunset policy, emit `Deprecation`
and `Sunset` headers from the day of deprecation, instrument usage so you can see
who is left, and contact them before the date rather than after.

## The library

`Asp.Versioning.Http` — the successor to `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Versioning` —
implements everything in this sector properly and adds things you would not build
yourself: version sets shared across endpoints, `MapToApiVersion` for
endpoint-level overrides, several `IApiVersionReader`s that can be combined,
automatic `api-supported-versions` and `api-deprecated-versions` response
headers, and OpenAPI integration that produces one document per version.

Use it. The reason to hand-build the mechanisms once is that the library's
concepts stop being opaque: a version reader is the filter you wrote in exercise
2, a version set is the group you wrote in exercise 1, and the deprecation
headers are exactly the ones you set in exercise 6.

What no library does is decide whether your change needs a version. That remains
a judgement about your clients, and it is the part of this subject worth actually
learning.

## Retiring, which is the part that never happens

Almost every API that supports an embarrassing number of versions got there the
same way: each version was introduced with a plan to retire the previous one, and
no version was ever retired. The reasons are always operational rather than
technical.

Nobody knows who is using it. Without per-version, per-caller usage metrics, the
question "can we turn off v1" has no answer, and in the absence of an answer the
default is always to wait. Instrumenting this is a day's work at the time the
version is created and impossible to do retroactively for callers who have
already stopped talking to you.

Nobody owns the announcement. `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers are emitted by
code; contacting the eleven remaining integrators is a person's job, and it is
nobody's job unless it is scheduled. The teams that succeed at retirement treat
the sunset date as a project milestone with an owner, not as a header value.

The retirement is all-or-nothing. Turning v1 off for everyone at once is a large,
scary, unrehearsed change. Turning it off for callers with zero traffic in the
last ninety days, then for internal callers, then for the rest, is four small
ones — and the first three are risk-free because you measured.

And the 410 is skipped. Deleting the routes is one line less work than keeping
them and answering 410, and it throws away the only message that reaches a client
who shows up eight months later. Keep the 410, keep it for years, and put the
successor in it.

## When not to version

**Do not version an internal API with one consumer you deploy alongside.** Change
both. The versioning machinery is a cost paid to avoid coordination, and you
already have coordination.

**Do not version to fix a bug.** If a response was wrong — a field misspelt in a
way nobody could have relied on, a status code that violated the spec — fixing it
in place is usually right, and announcing it is what makes it acceptable.
Versioning a bug means committing to reproduce it forever.

**Do not version for an experiment.** Feature flags and preview headers exist for
"this may change". A version implies stability; do not make that promise about
something you intend to move.

**Do not create a version per endpoint.** The unit of versioning should be the
API, or at most a bounded area of it. Per-endpoint versions produce a matrix
where nobody can say which combinations were ever tested.

## Further reading

- [ASP.NET Core API versioning](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnet-api-versioning/wiki)
- [RFC 8594 — The Sunset HTTP Header Field](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8594)
- [RFC 9110 — HTTP semantics, status codes](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)
- [System.Text.Json: handling missing and unmapped members](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/serialization/system-text-json/missing-members)
- [OpenAPI and versioned API documents](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/openapi/aspnetcore-openapi)

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — two versions in the path, one handler where nothing changed

Edit `src/Api/V3DA05_ApiVersioning/Ex1.cs`. The rate book is at the bottom of the
file: three lanes (`FEL-RTM`, `RTM-SIN`, `SIN-LAX`) and three quotes, each with a
base rate, a surcharge, a currency and a validity date.

Build two groups, `/v3da05/v1` and `/v3da05/v2`, and map:

- `GET /v3da05/v{n}/lanes` — **identical in both versions**, so map the *same
  handler method* into both groups. Returns the lane codes, ordinally ascending:
  `{"lanes":["FEL-RTM","RTM-SIN","SIN-LAX"]}`
- `GET /v3da05/v{n}/quotes/{id:int}` — different shapes:

v1:

```json
{"id":1,"lane":"FEL-RTM","rate":1450.00,"currency":"EUR"}
```

v2:

```json
{"id":1,"lane":"FEL-RTM","baseRate":1200.00,"surcharge":250.00,
 "total":1450.00,"currency":"EUR","validUntil":"2026-03-31"}
```

Unknown id → **404** in both.

v1 promised a single combined `rate` and no expiry. v2 splits it and adds the
date. Note that v1's `rate` must equal v2's `total` — the number did not change,
only how much of the calculation the client can see. That is what makes this a
shape change rather than a behaviour change, and it is the kind you can adapt
your way out of.

Do **not** copy the lookup logic into two methods. One `ListLanes` mapped twice,
and two projections over the same `Quote` record, is the whole exercise. Two
handlers that both compute a rate will diverge, and you will fix a bug in one of
them.

Also set `WithTags("v3da05-v1")` and `WithTags("v3da05-v2")` on the groups — the
tag is per-version metadata, and DA6 will use it to produce one OpenAPI document
per version.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da05_api_versioning ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A version in the path is a route prefix, and you already have the tool for
shared route prefixes with shared conventions. Nothing new is needed to version
this way, which is a large part of the argument for it.

## Hint 2

The same method into two groups:

    var v1 = app.MapGroup("/depot/v1");
    var v2 = app.MapGroup("/depot/v2");

    v1.MapGet("/regions", ListRegions);
    v2.MapGet("/regions", ListRegions);   // same delegate, two endpoints

Two `Endpoint` objects are built, each with its own metadata, both pointing at
one method.

## Hint 3

Write `Quote` once, then `ToV1` and `ToV2` as static projections. The decision
left to you: should `total` be computed in the projection or stored on `Quote`?
One of those answers survives a third version that redefines what counts toward
the total.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Check the arithmetic first: v1's `rate` and v2's `total` must be the same number
for the same quote. If they differ, you have accidentally shipped a behavioural
change wearing a shape change's clothes, which is the most expensive kind.

## Hint 2

If `/v3da05/v1/lanes` 404s, look at the group prefix and the mapped path
together. `MapGroup("/v3da05/v1/")` plus `MapGet("/lanes")` gives a doubled
slash in some route tables; keep the prefix without a trailing slash and every
mapped path with a leading one.

## Hint 3

Try writing the two quote endpoints as two full handlers with their own lookups,
then delete one and re-derive it from the shared record. The second version is
shorter, and more importantly it has one place where "what is a quote" is
decided. That refactoring instinct — push the versioning to the edge of the
system — is the thing this sector is really teaching.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — resolving a version from a header or a query string

Edit `src/Api/V3DA05_ApiVersioning/Ex2.cs`. One URL, `/v3da05/quotes/{id:int}`,
serving both shapes, with the version resolved from the request.

Write an endpoint filter, applied to a group at `/v3da05`, that:

1. reads `X-Api-Version` and `?api-version=`
2. if **both** are present and **differ** → **400** problem, `title` =
   `Conflicting API versions`, extensions `header` and `query`
3. if neither is present → version **1** (this exercise's default; ex8 revisits
   the choice)
4. if the value is not `1` or `2` → **400** problem, `title` = `Unsupported API
   version`, extensions `requested` (the raw string) and `supported` (`[1,2]`)
5. otherwise stores the version in `HttpContext.Items["v3da05-version"]`, sets
   the response header `api-supported-versions` to `1,2`, and calls `next`

The endpoint reads the version back out of `Items` and projects with the ex1
adapters.

Every response — including the 400s — must carry `Vary: X-Api-Version`.

Expected:

- no version indicators → 200 with the **v1** shape
- `X-Api-Version: 2` → 200 with the v2 shape
- `?api-version=2` → 200 with the v2 shape
- `X-Api-Version: 1` with `?api-version=2` → 400 `Conflicting API versions`
- `X-Api-Version: 9` → 400 `Unsupported API version`, `supported: [1,2]`
- `X-Api-Version: two` → 400 `Unsupported API version`, `requested: "two"`

Two things earn their place. The `supported` list turns a client's five-minute
fix into a one-minute one. And `Vary` is not optional: a shared cache that has
stored the v1 response for this URL will hand it to a v2 client unless you say
what the response depends on — which is the strongest practical argument for
putting the version in the path instead.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da05_api_versioning ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The version has to be known before the handler runs and has to be available
inside it. That is a filter plus `HttpContext.Items` — the same shape as the
trace list in DA1.

## Hint 2

Reading two sources with a defined precedence, and refusing a conflict:

    var header = http.Request.Headers["X-Api-Version"].ToString();
    var query = http.Request.Query["api-version"].ToString();

    if (header.Length > 0 && query.Length > 0 && header != query)
        return TypedResults.Problem(title: "Conflicting versions", statusCode: 400);

    var raw = header.Length > 0 ? header : query;

Note that a conflict is refused rather than resolved: a client sending both is a
client with a bug, and picking one for them hides it.

## Hint 3

Parse with `int.TryParse`, then check membership in the supported set — that way
`"two"` and `"9"` take the same path and both report `requested`. The decision
left to you: is `?api-version=1.0` the same as `1`? Decide before a client asks.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Set `Vary` first, before any early return, or your 400s will not carry it. A
cache that stores an error response without knowing what it varied on is a cache
that will replay that error to somebody else.

## Hint 2

If the default case returns the v2 shape, your "neither present" branch is
falling through to a `switch` whose default arm is v2. Make the default explicit
— `version = 1` — rather than relying on the arm order; ex8 will change this
value and you want exactly one place to change.

## Hint 3

Compare this exercise with ex1 honestly. You have written thirty lines of
mechanism to achieve what a route prefix did for free, and gained one URL per
resource. That is the actual trade, and knowing its size is what lets you argue

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — negotiating a representation with `Accept`

Edit `src/Api/V3DA05_ApiVersioning/Ex3.cs`. Map
`GET /v3da05/media/quotes/{id:int}` and take the version from the **media type
parameter** in `Accept`.

Parse the header properly with `MediaTypeHeaderValue.TryParseList`, not with
`Split(',')`. Walk the parsed candidates in order and take the first whose media
type is `application/json` or `*/*`:

- that candidate has no `v` parameter → version **1**
- `v=1` or `v=2` → that version
- `v` present and anything else → **406**, `title` = `Unsupported representation`,
  extensions `requested` and `supported`
- no `Accept` header at all → version 1
- no candidate matches `application/json` or `*/*` → **406**, `title` = `Only
  application/json is available`

Set the response `Content-Type` to `application/json; v=<n>` on success, so the
client can see which representation it actually got.

Expected:

- no `Accept` → 200, v1 shape, `Content-Type: application/json; v=1`
- `Accept: application/json` → 200, v1
- `Accept: application/json; v=2` → 200, v2 shape,
  `Content-Type: application/json; v=2`
- `Accept: application/json; v=9` → **406**
- `Accept: application/xml` → **406** `Only application/json is available`
- `Accept: application/xml, application/json; v=2` → 200, v2 — the xml candidate
  is skipped, not fatal

406 rather than 400 is the deliberate difference from ex2. A version in a header
of your own invention is an input you defined, and a bad one is a malformed
request. A version in `Accept` is a *representation request*, and being unable to
produce it is exactly what 406 Not Acceptable means. Same underlying condition,
different status, because the client asked a different question.

The last row is why hand-parsing fails. `Accept` is an ordered list of candidates
with optional quality values, and a client that lists a format you cannot produce
alongside one you can is making a perfectly reasonable request.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da05_api_versioning ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Accept` is a list, not a string. Any solution that looks for the substring
`"v=2"` gets the simple cases right and the realistic ones wrong.

## Hint 2

Parsing it, and reading a parameter:

    if (!MediaTypeHeaderValue.TryParseList(request.Headers.Accept, out var candidates))
        return null;

    foreach (var candidate in candidates)
    {
        if (candidate.MediaType != "application/json" && candidate.MediaType != "*/*")
            continue;

        var v = candidate.Parameters
            .FirstOrDefault(p => p.Name.Equals("v", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase));
        …
    }

`MediaTypeHeaderValue` lives in `Microsoft.Net.Http.Headers`, not
`System.Net.Http.Headers` — the ASP.NET Core one is the allocation-conscious
version.

## Hint 3

Three outcomes from the parse — a version, "not acceptable at all", and
"unsupported version" — so return something that can express all three rather
than an `int?`. The decision left to you: should `q` values be honoured, so that
`application/json;v=2;q=0.1, application/json;v=1;q=0.9` prefers v1? Correct HTTP
says yes; almost nobody implements it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Test the mixed header early — `application/xml, application/json; v=2`. It is the
one that separates a parser from a substring search, and it is what a browser or
a generated client will actually send.

## Hint 2

If `Accept: application/json` returns a 406, your "no `v` parameter" branch is
falling into the unsupported case. Absent and invalid are different: absent means
the client has no opinion and should get the default, invalid means they asked
for something that does not exist.

## Hint 3

Note what the `Content-Type` response header buys. Without it a client cannot
tell whether its `v=2` was honoured or quietly defaulted, and "it worked in
staging" incidents come from exactly that ambiguity. Echoing the negotiated
representation is cheap and it makes the negotiation observable — the same
instinct as `api-supported-versions` in ex2.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — adding a field, and proving nobody broke

Edit `src/Api/V3DA05_ApiVersioning/Ex4.cs`. The business wants two additions to
the quote API, and the point of the exercise is that **neither needs a version**.

Map `POST /v3da05/additive/quotes` taking

```csharp
record QuoteRequest(string Lane, int Weight, string? ServiceLevel)
```

`ServiceLevel` is the new **optional request field**. Its default must preserve
the previous behaviour exactly: absent or null means `standard`. Accepted values
are `standard` and `express`; `express` multiplies the surcharge by 2. Anything
else → 400 validation problem keyed `"serviceLevel"`.

The response is the new **additive response field**, `carbonKg`, added to *both*
shapes:

v1:

```json
{"id":4,"lane":"FEL-RTM","rate":1450.00,"currency":"EUR","carbonKg":312.5}
```

v2 keeps all its existing members and gains the same `carbonKg`.

Then map `GET /v3da05/additive/contract/{version:int}` returning the member names
of that version's response shape, ordinally ordered, so the gate can assert that
**every v1 member from ex1 is still present** and only `carbonKg` was added:

```json
{"version":1,"members":["carbonKg","currency","id","lane","rate"]}
```

The gate runs ex1's v1 assertions against this endpoint's v1 output and expects
them all to pass. That is the demonstration: a v1 client written before
`carbonKg` existed deserialises this response, ignores the member it does not
know, and continues working. No version bump, no migration, no email.

Two conditions make that true, and both are yours to maintain. The client must be
a tolerant reader — `System.Text.Json` is by default, and a client that set
`UnmappedMemberHandling.Disallow` has opted out. And the new request field's
default must reproduce the old behaviour precisely: if `standard` charged
differently from "no service level specified", you would have made a breaking
change wearing an optional field's clothes.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da05_api_versioning ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two changes, one rule: after the change, every request that used to work must
still produce the same answer. Test that property directly rather than reasoning

## Hint 2

A default that preserves behaviour:

    var level = body.ServiceLevel ?? "standard";
    if (level is not ("standard" or "express"))
        return TypedResults.ValidationProblem(new Dictionary<string, string[]>
        {
            ["serviceLevel"] = ["standard or express."],

## Hint 1

Run ex1's v1 expectations against this endpoint before you add anything, then

## Hint 2

If `serviceLevel: ""` is accepted, your coalesce is doing more than you meant —

## Hint 3

## Exercise 5 — one domain object, three promised shapes

Edit `src/Api/V3DA05_ApiVersioning/Ex5.cs`. A third version exists now, and the
`if (version == 1) … else …` in ex2 has stopped scaling.

Define three **named DTO records** — not anonymous types — and one adapter each:

```csharp
public record QuoteV1(int Id, string Lane, decimal Rate, string Currency);
public record QuoteV2(int Id, string Lane, decimal BaseRate, decimal Surcharge,
                      decimal Total, string Currency, string ValidUntil);
public record QuoteV3(string Id, string Lane, Money Total, Money[] Components,
                      string ValidUntil);
public record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency);
```

v3 makes two genuinely breaking changes on purpose: `id` becomes a **string**
(`"q-1"`), and money becomes an object with an explicit currency rather than a
bare decimal alongside a currency field. Both are the sort of change that arrives
when an API grows a second currency or a second id space.

Register the adapters in a `Dictionary<int, Func<Quote, object>>` and map
`GET /v3da05/adapt/quotes/{id:int}`, resolving the version with the ex2 filter
mechanism extended to accept `3`.

Expected for quote 1:

- v1: `{"id":1,"lane":"FEL-RTM","rate":1450.00,"currency":"EUR"}`
- v2: unchanged from ex1
- v3: `{"id":"q-1","lane":"FEL-RTM","total":{"amount":1450.00,"currency":"EUR"},
  "components":[{"amount":1200.00,"currency":"EUR"},
  {"amount":250.00,"currency":"EUR"}],"validUntil":"2026-03-31"}`

Also map `GET /v3da05/adapt/versions` returning `{"versions":[1,2,3]}` **derived
from the dictionary's keys**, ordered ascending — so adding a version is one
dictionary entry and the discovery endpoint follows automatically.

The shape to notice: the handler no longer knows how many versions exist. It
looks one up and calls it. Adding v4 touches one file and adds one function;
retiring v1 deletes one function and one entry. Compare that with a handler
containing three branches, where every version's peculiarities are interleaved
with every other's.

The limit of the pattern is worth stating too. Adapters map *shapes*. If v3 also
rounded money differently from v2, no adapter could express it — that difference
lives in the domain, and the honest fix is a parameter, not a mapping.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da05_api_versioning ex5
```

Write the v3 expected JSON out by hand before coding, especially the nested

## Hint 2

## Hint 3

Try adding a v4 that renames `lane` to `corridor` and see how much you touch: one

Then imagine the same change in a three-branch handler. That difference is not
aesthetic — it is the difference between a version being a contained cost and
being a tax on every future edit.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — telling clients a version is going away

Edit `src/Api/V3DA05_ApiVersioning/Ex6.cs`. Deprecation is a conversation that has
to start long before the shutdown, and it has standard headers so that gateways
and generated clients can surface it without reading your blog.

Build three groups under `/v3da05/lifecycle`: `/v1`, `/v2` and `/v3`, each with a
`GET /quotes/{id:int}` using the ex5 adapters.

Apply a **group convention** to `/v1` — not a line in each handler — that sets, on
every response including errors:

```
Deprecation: Wed, 01 Jan 2025 00:00:00 GMT
Sunset: Tue, 01 Jul 2025 00:00:00 GMT
Link: </v3da05/lifecycle/docs/v1-to-v3>; rel="deprecation"; type="text/html"
api-deprecated-versions: 1
```

Apply to `/v2` only `api-deprecated-versions:` — empty is wrong, so omit the
header entirely on v2 and v3.

All three groups set `api-supported-versions: 1,2,3`.

Then map `GET /v3da05/lifecycle/versions` returning:

```json
{"versions":[{"version":1,"status":"deprecated","sunset":"2025-07-01"},
             {"version":2,"status":"supported","sunset":null},
             {"version":3,"status":"current","sunset":null}]}
```

Expected: a v1 response carries all four headers and a normal 200 body; a 404
from v1 carries them too; v2 and v3 responses carry `api-supported-versions` and
no deprecation headers.

Three details are the exercise.

The headers go on **errors as well as successes**, which is why this is a group
convention rather than something the projection does. A client polling a v1
endpoint that mostly 404s should still learn the version is going away.

`Sunset` is an HTTP-date, per RFC 8594 — `Tue, 01 Jul 2025 00:00:00 GMT`, not
`2025-07-01`. Machine-readable means a specific machine-readable format.

And a deprecated version must still **work**. Deprecation is an announcement, not
a degradation; slowing v1 down or making it flaky to encourage migration converts
a planned change into an incident, and clients respond by distrusting every
announcement you make afterwards.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da05_api_versioning ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every response from one version needs the same four headers. That is a
per-version cross-cutting concern, and you already know where those live.

## Hint 2

Formatting an HTTP-date correctly:

    var sunset = new DateTimeOffset(2025, 7, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero);
    headers["Sunset"] = sunset.ToString("R");     // Tue, 01 Jul 2025 00:00:00 GMT

The `"R"` round-trip format is RFC 1123, which is what HTTP-date means. Hand-
formatting it will get the day name wrong eventually.

## Hint 3

Set the headers *before* `await next(context)` so they are present regardless of
what the handler returns. The decision left to you: should the `Link` header use
`rel="deprecation"` or `rel="sunset"`? Both are registered; look at what each one
is defined to point at and pick the one you can actually host.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Test the 404 path deliberately. Ask v1 for quote 99 and check all four headers
are on the response. If they are missing, you set them after `next` and returned
early somewhere, or you set them inside the success projection.

## Hint 2

If the `Sunset` header comes back as `07/01/2025 00:00:00`, you formatted with
the current culture. HTTP dates are always English and always GMT; `"R"` on a
`DateTimeOffset` handles both, and `DateTime.Now.ToString("R")` quietly does not
because it will not be UTC.

## Hint 3

Think about what happens next in the real timeline. You have announced a sunset
date; now you need to know who is still on v1 as it approaches. That means
counting v1 requests per client, which means a per-version metric and a way to
identify callers — usually the API key or `sub` from DA3. A sunset you cannot
measure compliance with is a sunset you will not dare to enforce, and the version
lives forever.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — retiring a version so the client knows what to do

Edit `src/Api/V3DA05_ApiVersioning/Ex7.cs`. The sunset date has passed. v1 is
gone, and how it is gone matters.

Map a **catch-all** for the retired version:

```
/v3da05/retired/v1/{**rest}
```

for **every** HTTP method — use `MapMethods` with `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`,
`DELETE` — answering **410 Gone** with `application/problem+json`:

```json
{"title":"API version 1 has been retired","status":410,
 "retiredOn":"2025-07-01","successor":"/v3da05/retired/v2",
 "requestedPath":"/v3da05/retired/v1/quotes/1"}
```

and a response header `Link: </v3da05/retired/v2>; rel="successor-version"`.

Map `/v3da05/retired/v2/quotes/{id:int}` normally, returning the `QuoteV2` shape.

Expected: `GET /v3da05/retired/v1/quotes/1` → 410 with the body above;
`POST /v3da05/retired/v1/anything` → 410; `GET /v3da05/retired/v2/quotes/1` →
200; `GET /v3da05/retired/v3/quotes/1` → **404**, because v3 never existed here
and that is a different fact.

The distinction the exercise turns on: 404 says "no such thing, check your URL",
and 410 says "this existed, it is gone, here is where to go". A client receiving
404 will re-read your documentation looking for a typo. A client receiving 410
with a `successor` will open a migration ticket. Same failed request, entirely
different next hour for whoever is on call at their end.

Keeping the route registered is what makes 410 possible at all. Deleting the v1
endpoints gives you 404 for free and throws away the last, most useful message
you will ever send those clients.

One production note the gate cannot check: keep the 410 for a long time. The
whole value is that it reaches a client who has not looked at your API in a year,
and a route that costs nothing to keep should outlive the code it replaced by
years, not weeks.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da05_api_versioning ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The version is gone; the *route* is not. Something still has to answer every URL
that used to work, and what it answers is the whole point.

## Hint 2

A catch-all across methods:

    app.MapMethods("/api/v1/{**rest}",
        ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"],
        (string? rest, HttpContext http) => Gone(http));

`{**rest}` is the catch-all parameter: it matches the remainder of the path
including slashes, and it has the lowest routing precedence, so a real v2 route
declared anywhere still wins.

## Hint 3

`http.Request.Path` gives you the full requested path for the `requestedPath`
member. The decision left to you: should the 410 include the `Sunset` header
again? It is past, so it is arguably historical rather than a warning — say what
a client library would do with each answer.

## Hint 1

Try the v3 request first and confirm it is a 404. If your catch-all is mounted at

410, and you have started telling clients that things which never existed have

## Hint 2

If `POST` gets a 405 rather than a 410, you mapped with `MapGet`. Routing matched

## Hint 3

Sketch the whole timeline the three exercises have covered: v1 ships; v2 ships

supporting a version from six years ago is almost never that retiring it was
hard — it is that nobody started the conversation at step two.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — what an unversioned request should get

Edit `src/Api/V3DA05_ApiVersioning/Ex8.cs`. Every API has a policy for requests
that do not state a version, and most have it by accident. Implement all three
deliberately and compare them.

Define:

```csharp
public enum DefaultVersionPolicy { Latest, Oldest, Refuse }
```

and map `GET /v3da05/default/{policy}/quotes/{id:int}` where `{policy}` is
`latest`, `oldest` or `refuse`. Supported versions are 1, 2 and 3. When
`X-Api-Version` is present and valid, it is honoured under all three policies.
When it is **absent**:

- `latest` → serve **v3**, response header `api-version: 3` and
  `api-version-source: default-latest`
- `oldest` → serve **v1**, `api-version: 1`, `api-version-source:
  default-oldest`
- `refuse` → **400** problem, `title` = `An API version is required`, extensions
  `supported` (`[1,2,3]`) and `how` (`"Send X-Api-Version or ?api-version"`)

When the header **is** present, `api-version-source` is `request` under all three.

Then map `GET /v3da05/default/policies` returning a description of each, so the
gate can assert the trade-offs are written down somewhere:

```json
{"policies":[
 {"policy":"latest","unversionedGets":3,"breaksOnRelease":true},
 {"policy":"oldest","unversionedGets":1,"breaksOnRelease":false},
 {"policy":"refuse","unversionedGets":null,"breaksOnRelease":false}]}
```

Now the argument, which is the actual content of this exercise.

**Latest** is what most people build by accident, and it is the only one that can
break a working client with no code change on their side: they wrote an
unversioned call against v1, you shipped v3, and their integration changed
underneath them. It is defensible only while every client is you.

**Oldest** never breaks anyone and quietly gives new integrators the behaviour
you were trying to move away from — they will write against v1, discover v3 six
months later, and migrate a codebase that need never have used v1.

**Refuse** is the strictest and, for anything internal, the kindest: no client can
be surprised, because no client is guessing. Its cost is real and mostly social —
the first `curl` anybody tries fails, and an API whose "hello world" fails feels
hostile.

The `api-version` and `api-version-source` response headers are the part to keep
whichever policy you pick. A client that can see which version it got, and
whether it asked for it, can diagnose in seconds what would otherwise be a
support thread.

```
uv run dojo test dotnet v3da05_api_versioning ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One resolution function with a policy parameter, three routes into it. If you
find yourself writing three resolvers, the policies have leaked into the rest of
the handler.

## Hint 2

Reporting the provenance, not just the value:

    var (version, source) = raw.Length > 0
        ? (int.Parse(raw), "request")
        : policy switch
        {
            DefaultVersionPolicy.Latest => (Supported.Max(), "default-latest"),
            DefaultVersionPolicy.Oldest => (Supported.Min(), "default-oldest"),
            _ => (0, "refuse"),

`Supported.Max()` rather than a hard-coded 3 means adding v4 does not silently

## Hint 3

The `refuse` branch returns before any lookup. The decision left to you: should

Run each policy with and without the header, six requests, and read the two

If `latest` is serving v2, `Supported.Max()` is reading a stale collection or you

## Hint 3

Decide what you would actually pick and be able to defend it in one sentence. A
